Learning Dynamics of On-policy Distillation

Guan Zhe Hong Affiliation: University of Oxford    Sumeet R. Motwani Affiliation: University of Oxford    Liang Chen Affiliation: EPFL    Yangchen Pan Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong    Junchi Yu Affiliation: University of Oxford    Jialin Yu Affiliation: University of Oxford    Philip H.S. Torr Affiliation: University of Oxford    Yi Ren Affiliation: University of Oxford
Abstract

On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for language-model post-training, combining dense teacher supervision with training on student-generated trajectories. This creates a feedback loop where each update changes the student and thereby the training distribution that generates subsequent updates. Yet, how this feedback shapes learning and generalization remains poorly understood. We conduct a mechanistic analysis of OPD’s learning dynamics, distinguishing the two feedback loop stages: conversion of the distillation signal into parameter updates, and broadcast through which these updates change predictions across prefixes and reshape the rollout distribution. This framework helps us understand both limited student responsiveness despite substantial teacher-student disagreement, and degeneration when updates that improve local teacher agreement also increase the probability of unsuccessful continuations, exposing the student to unreliable supervision in subsequent rollouts. Finally, we show that offline distillation can prepare a student for OPD without significantly improving immediate held-out accuracy. While OPD alone may degrade generation, it can yield substantial accuracy gains after sufficient offline preparation. Together, our results connect teacher supervision, student geometry, and the evolving rollout distribution in determining the learning dynamics of OPD and its effects on downstream performance.

1 Introduction

On-policy distillation (OPD) is becoming an important component of language-model post-training (Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Song and Zheng, 2026a). By matching a teacher’s next-token distributions at student-generated prefixes, it combines dense supervision with training on the states the student actually visits (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024). Yet, how this local supervision becomes useful learning over an evolving training distribution remains insufficiently understood. It is therefore important to theoretically understand both the conditions under which OPD improves generalization and its role alongside offline distillation.

The difficulty is that each OPD update changes both the student’s current behavior and the prefixes on which it will subsequently learn. Reducing teacher-student divergence on currently supervised predictions does not necessarily produce parameters from which further updates are useful (Li et al., 2026b; Armandpour et al., 2026). Modelling this requires a view of how supervision changes behavior beyond the current batch and how that impacts learning at later stages. We conduct a mechanistic analysis, aided by a first-principles account, of OPD learning dynamics to study this process, explain existing empirical challenges, and justify their empirical diagnostics and fixes.

We first characterize how the teacher-student log-probability difference can lead to meaningful weight updates, which depends on the overlap between the distillation signal and the logit-space directions the student’s current parameters can express. We then describe how learning at one prefix affects predictions at future ones through their dependence on shared parameter directions. We formalize this broadcast relationship through the student’s tangent kernel between the two prefixes, building on Ren and Sutherland (2025); Malladi et al. (2023). Finally, we connect each update to its effect on the outcomes of student-generated sequences. The effect of these updates in broader settings also depends on what the training data covers: matching the teacher on narrow tasks may transfer only the capabilities that those tasks exercise. Integrating these effects over training characterizes what OPD can reach from a given starting point, accounting for how much successive updates improve or degrade performance.

This framework helps us understand two primary failure modes of OPD: stagnation under stronger teachers and degeneration into incoherent outputs (Li et al., 2026b; Fu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). In the first case, despite substantial teacher–student log-probability differences, we show that the initial distillation signal can induce smaller parameter gradients as training proceeds, contributing to stalled improvement. In the second case, updates that reduce teacher–student disagreement at supervised prefixes also change predictions at other prefixes through shared parameters. These changes can shift the rollout distribution toward continuations the student cannot execute reliably, making those unstable continuations the source of subsequent supervision, making the teacher struggle to rescue, let alone improve the student. We illustrate the dynamical process of OPD and its possible failure modes in Figure 1 (we will elaborate on the intuitions behind this further in Section 3.1).

The dependence of OPD on the student sustaining stable rollouts (prefixes) which induce meaningful supervision motivates offline preparation. Here, the weak student is first forced to visit the teacher’s prefixes and learn predictions there, enabling the subsequent OPD process to sustain productive learning as the student exposes finer correction opportunities to the teacher, while maintaining stabler and more recoverable changes in its rollout distribution. Across Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.1 models on AIME 2024 and 2025 problems, we find that under sufficient offline training, the subsequent OPD phase substantially improve pass@kk (for kk up to 32) and per-problem reliability compared to offline training alone. In the rest of the paper, we present these results and insights organized under the following three questions. What determines the conversion of teacher supervision into policy motion (Section 3.2)? Does the broadcast of these updates across prefixes improve subsequent reasoning or steer the student toward unreliable continuations and supervision (Section 3.3)? Can offline preparation strengthen the student’s continuation ability and enable productive on-policy learning (3.4)?

Related works. We briefly discuss related works here, and leave the expanded version to Appendix Appendix B. On-policy distillation. Training on learner-generated states with expert feedback is a classical approach to addressing distribution shift in imitation learning (Ross et al., 2011), applied to autoregressive distillation by Lin et al. (2020). Gu et al. (2024) develop reverse-KL distillation using student rollouts, while Agarwal et al. (2024) unify on-policy and off-policy training across multiple divergences. Lu and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) demonstrate its effectiveness for reasoning and personalization in language-model post-training. More recently, Yang et al. (2026) interpret OPD as dense KL-constrained reinforcement learning and introduce reward extrapolation. Empirical studies identify teacher-student compatibility on student prefixes as important factors in transfer and training failure (Li et al., 2026b; Fu et al., 2026).

Learning dynamics of finetuning. Kernel-based analyses connect parameter updates to changes in language-model predictions (Malladi et al., 2023). Ren and Sutherland (2025) decompose per-step prediction changes using the loss gradient and empirical tangent kernel, analyzing confidence dynamics in SFT and DPO (Rafailov et al., 2024). Tomihari (2026) study how RL updates propagate across examples, while Shen et al. (2026) identify persistent low-dimensional subspaces in OPD updates. Building on these perspectives, we connect the student’s evolving tangent kernel to its response to teacher supervision, the quality of its continuations, and the resulting distribution of future training prefixes. This distinguishes limited response to supervision from policy changes that worsen generation, and explains how either can shape subsequent learning.

2 Setup

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own samples. The student generates a continuation from a prompt. At every prefix of that continuation, the training loss pulls the student’s next-token distribution toward the next-token distribution of a fixed teacher (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). This section fixes the notation for the objects that recur in the paper, including the policies, the source distribution that a run trains on, the request field that the teacher induces on that source, and the evaluation targets that we score runs against.

Policies and rollouts.

A prefix ss is a prompt followed by a partial continuation. Prefixes range over a space 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and tokens range over a finite vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The student has parameters θ∈ℝd\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, logits zθ​(s)∈ℝ|𝒱|z_{\theta}(s)\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}, and next-token distribution pθ​(a∣s)=softmax​(zθ​(s))ap_{\theta}(a\mid s)=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{\theta}(s))_{a}. The teacher q(⋅∣s)q(\cdot\mid s) is fixed throughout training. Training proceeds in steps t=0,1,2,…t=0,1,2,\ldots. Gradient flow, the continuous-time version of the training process, has the update rule θ˙t=ut\dot{\theta}_{t}=u_{t}. For discrete gradient steps this gives a first-order local approximation Section C.2. Two distributions share the student’s weights. The model policy ptp_{t} is the distribution that the loss acts on. The rollout policy πt=𝒢⁡[pt]\pi_{t}=\mathcal{G}[p_{t}] is the distribution that generates the samples (the transform 𝒢\mathcal{G} collects the temperature, end-of-sequence conventions, etc). We sample prompts b∼βb\sim\beta and continue them under πt\pi_{t}. The step-tt rollout population is Πt​(ξ)=β⁡(b)​∏jπt​(aj∣sj)\Pi_{t}(\xi)=\beta(b)\prod_{j}\pi_{t}(a_{j}\mid s_{j}) for a trajectory ξ=(b,a0,a1,…)\xi=(b,a_{0},a_{1},\ldots), with s0=bs_{0}=b and sj+1=sj⊕ajs_{j+1}=s_{j}\oplus a_{j} up to termination or the cap. The training source distribution μt=ℳ⁡(Πt)\mu_{t}=\mathcal{M}(\Pi_{t}) is the distribution over prefixes that the model trains on (ℳ\mathcal{M} normalizes over the rollouts to form the probability distribution).

Loss, request field, and update.

For reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence, the per-prefix loss is ct(s)=DKL(pt(⋅∣s)∥q(⋅∣s))c_{t}(s)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{t}(\cdot\mid s)\,\|\,q(\cdot\mid s)\right). It captures the student-teacher disagreement on a given prefix. The product Γt=μt​Bt\Gamma_{t}=\mu_{t}B_{t}, visitation times request, is the request population. See Section C.1 for further details on the setup.

3 The Learning Dynamics of the OPD loop

3.1 The OPD loop and the response law

Recall that Πt\Pi_{t} denotes the distribution of student rollouts and μt=ℳ⁡(Πt)\mu_{t}=\mathcal{M}(\Pi_{t}) the distribution of prefixes used by the loss. At a sampled prefix s∼μts\sim\mu_{t}, the student ptp_{t} and the teacher qq supply the request Bt​(s)=−∇zt​(s)ct​(s)B_{t}(s)=-\nabla_{z_{t}(s)}c_{t}(s). The request population Γt​(s)=μt​(s)​Bt​(s)\Gamma_{t}(s)=\mu_{t}(s)B_{t}(s) specifies what change it requests on a prefix, across the rollout disitribution μt\mu_{t}. These requests then convert into parameter motion through the tangent map Φt​(s)=∇θzt​(s)\Phi_{t}(s)=\nabla_{\theta}z_{t}(s), which changes the future policy and rollouts. More explicitly, one training step follows

Πt⏟rollouts→ℳμt⏟source→𝑞Γt=μt​Bt⏟weighted requests→ΦΔ​θt⏟parameter step→responseΔ​log⁡pt​(⋅)⏟policy changes⟶Πt+1⏟next rollouts\underbrace{\Pi_{t}}_{\text{rollouts}}\xrightarrow{\;\mathcal{M}\;}\underbrace{\mu_{t}}_{\text{source}}\xrightarrow{\;q\;}\underbrace{\Gamma_{t}=\mu_{t}B_{t}}_{\text{weighted requests}}\xrightarrow{\;\Phi\;}\underbrace{\Delta\theta_{t}}_{\text{parameter step}}\xrightarrow{\;\text{response}\;}\underbrace{\Delta\log p_{t}(\cdot)}_{\text{policy changes}}\longrightarrow\underbrace{\Pi_{t+1}}_{\text{next rollouts}}

Local requests shape future motion.

Training imposes the gradient-based update ut=𝔼μt​[Φt​(s)⊤​Bt​(s)]u_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{t}}[\Phi_{t}(s)^{\top}B_{t}(s)]. For a gradient step Δ​θt=η​ut\Delta\theta_{t}=\eta u_{t}, the response at any receiver prefix xx is

Δpt(a∣x)=η∑sμt​(s)⏟source weight[𝖠tp​(x)⏟normalizationKt​(x,s)⏟student coupling​Bt​(s)⏟request⏞Δzt(x): logit response]a+O(η2),\Delta p_{t}(a\mid x)=\eta\sum_{s}\underbrace{\mu_{t}(s)}_{\text{source weight}}\Big[\underbrace{\mathsf{A}_{t}^{p}(x)}_{\text{normalization}}\;\overbrace{\underbrace{K_{t}(x,s)}_{\text{student coupling}}\;\underbrace{B_{t}(s)}_{\text{request}}}^{\Delta z_{t}(x)\text{: logit response}}\Big]_{a}+O(\eta^{2}), (2)

where Kt​(x,s)=Φt​(x)​Φt​(s)⊤K_{t}(x,s)=\Phi_{t}(x)\Phi_{t}(s)^{\top} and 𝖠tp(x)=I−𝟏pt(⋅∣x)⊤\mathsf{A}_{t}^{p}(x)=I-\mathbf{1}p_{t}(\cdot\mid x)^{\top}. The kernel KtK_{t} measures how source and receiver logits move together through shared parameters; 𝖠tp\mathsf{A}_{t}^{p} converts logit motion into log-probability motion. Therefore, the model’s prediction at any “receiver” prefix xx can change without appearing in the training batch.

In particular, since every prefix xx in a future rollout (from the future policy) is a receiver, (1) OPD updates will affect local per-prefix predictions of the student, captured by the logit motion z˙​(x)\dot{z}(x) and policy motion ∂logp(⋅∣x)\partial\log p(\cdot\mid x), (2) the updates will also shape which prefixes the student visits (changed μ\mu) and expose to teacher supervision (changed Γ\Gamma), as the policy motion along the ancestor tokens of any prefix xx accumulate to change its reach-probability.

Let us look at the illustrative process in Figure 1. Intuitively, imagine that the earlier requests locally promote the student to reason more and in specific manners (for instance, by requesting more “wait”-based backtracking, suppressing early “Answer:” commitment, asking for a specific theorem, and so on). Due to the autoregressive nature of the policies, this will not only affect how likely the student emits specific tokens such as “wait” or “answer:” in a future rollout of the student, but will also alter the overall rollout distribution, by lengthening the reasoning trace, exposing new reasoning sub-trajectories, different errors, etc. In the benign case, such online dynamics can be beneficial, as the teacher can correct the student in real time as if in a “tutorial” session.

However, one can also imagine that such a dynamical process can be quite fragile for a ill-prepared student. A weak student’s tangent map Φ\Phi simply might not be very sensitive to the requests, resulting in limited motion propagated from training to future prefixes via kernel KK, thus limited changes in task accuracy. Moreover, even if there is substantial motion, such motion can be harmful. Taking our analogy further, an ill-prepared student which has not “gone to class before the tutorial” might benefit very little from online corrections on its own rollouts and even become more confused. That is, the ill-prepared student which has not been pretrained properly on the task and sustain sufficiently strong rollouts might only mimic superficial local patterns requested by the teacher, and push its rollout population μ\mu towards chaos, which can then be hard for the teacher to generate the right request population Γ\Gamma to even rescue, let alone improve.

The rest of our analysis builds on the OPD loop and the response law to make precise the above intuitions, complemented by empirical analysis of real OPD runs, and examine how offline-distillation preparation before OPD helps alleviate the problems for weak student models. Section 3.2 (conversion) studies the student’s response to the supervised requests, which primarily concerns whether and how well a student model can convert different request populations Γ\Gamma (from different teachers) into policy motion z˙\dot{z} along the request fields. We develop early-training diagnostics of OPD runs from this perspective. Section 3.3 (broadcast) then focuses on where policy motion z˙\dot{z} goes and how it influences future training sources μ\mu, and analyze how and why policy motion which improves local per-prefix readouts (such as training loss) might not make positive progress on terminal readouts such as answer accuracy. Motivated by the failure mechanisms, we then show in Section 3.4, across Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.1 models, that with sufficient offline preparation, OPD runs improve pooled held-out accuracy (up to pass@32) and aggregate per-problem reliability on AIME 2024 and 2025 problems.

In the rest of this section, we primarily rely on the continuous gradient flow for cleaner theoretical discussions. Please see Section C.2 for further details on the finite step approximations.

3.2 Conversion: Teacher requests and the student’s responsiveness

A strong teacher can transfer little. We open with an intriguing empirical puzzle identified in the OPD community (Li et al., 2026b): a larger (same-family) teacher can transfer less than an RL-trained sibling even when they are nearly matched in bechmark performance, and Li et al. (2026b) suggests cancellation among token-level gradient signals as a possible explanation. We revisit this comparison at 1.5B and 7B (Figure 2), holding the starting DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen student and OPD recipe fixed within each scale. JustRL-1.5B and AceReason-Nemotron-7B yield substantial gains, whereas the larger DeepSeek-7B and DeepSeek-14B teachers transfer little throughout training despite higher benchmark scores (Section D.1). We call these runs healthy and stalled. We find that the teachers’ request fields differ substantially in semantic functions, and that the student’s responsiveness to these requests separates in two axes: coherence of the gradient signals, and kernel adaptation toward the requests. Along the way, we develop early-training diagnostics that help reveal the “request-conversion” health of a training run.

How do the request fields differ?

As we see in the OPD update loop in Section 3.1, the teacher’s request population Γt\Gamma_{t} at time 0 “kickstart” the whole learning process, from which the shared-parameter student model propagates into policy motion via its kernel KtK_{t}. Since the student starts out to be the same while the teachers are different across the healthy and stalled runs, their request fields become the natural entry point for our analysis.

On fixed initial-student rollouts, Figure 3 compares where each teacher’s largest-normed requests occur. (a) shows the coarse tendencies of the semantics of the requests as we move up the request-norm percentile, while (b) and (c) show the finer semantic categories and contrast the teachers’ distinct request fields. We find that the RL-sibling teachers increasingly emphasize reasoning-management and initiating positions, while the larger teachers place relatively more of their strongest requests at technically oriented (e.g. digit-bearing, recalling mathematical fact) positions. This separation connects to findings in the reasoning-interpretability community, that RL tends to improve how well the model “orchestrates” the base reasoning mechanisms (including epistemic control abilities) (Venhoff et al., 2025a). Full setup and analysis results are in Section D.2.

From requests to motion.

Figure 3 shows that the healthy and stalled teachers provide systematically different request fields in the large-normed stratum, but this alone does not help us understand which teacher’s request field converts better into policy motion along along the request field. Recall that for a prefix population ν\nu, the gradient is gt​(s)=Φt​(s)⊤​Bt​(s)g_{t}(s)=\Phi_{t}(s)^{\top}B_{t}(s) in terms of the tangent map and the request, ut=𝔼ν​gt​(s)u_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}g_{t}(s) the average gradient, and Pt=𝔼ν​‖Bt​(s)‖2P_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\|B_{t}(s)\|^{2} the request norm, or “pressure” (recall BB is the request field induced by the teacher-student disagreement). (4)

Accessibility averages the self-kernel Rayleigh coefficients B​(s)⊤​K​(s,s)​B​(s)/‖B⁡(s)‖2B(s)^{\top}K(s,s)B(s)/\|B(s)\|^{2}, weighted by request energy: it measures how responsive the student’s tangent map Φ⁡(s)\Phi(s) is to the requests B⁡(s)B(s). Coherence measures how well the resulting parameter updates g⁡(s)=Φ​(s)⊤​B​(s)g(s)=\Phi(s)^{\top}B(s) combine: aligned updates reinforce one another, while cancellation lowers CC. Thus “conversion” of requests into parameter-update-induced policy motion not only depend on pressure 𝔼ν​‖Bt​(s)‖2\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\|B_{t}(s)\|^{2}, but even if two runs have similar gradient norm with high pressure, the requests need not convert efficiently due to low accessibility (poor parameter-level motion per unit request norm at a prefix) or coherence (poor cross-prefix aggregation of parameter motion). The deeper geometric interpretations and derivations are in Section C.3. We now examine what the actual training runs reveal.

Coherence contrasts at 7B.

At 7B, healthy requests have near equal accessibility as the stalled requests but 2.752.75–3.24×3.24\times higher coherence, yielding 2.272.27–2.62×2.62\times higher collective gain Ξ\Xi across the two sampled high-strength strata (Figure 4(a)). Therefore, even though the gradient norms across the healthy and stalled runs are similar, we see that it is the greater pressure in the stalled run which masks the weaker coherence of the update forces for the stalled run. For this 7B case, the gradient-incoherence conjecture in Li et al. (2026b) is corroborated.

Evolving accessibility contrasts at 1.5B.

At 1.5B the mechanism is richer: initial accessibility is similar and coherence differs less; while we do see greater pressure for the healthy run (roughly 22–2.7×2.7\times, which yields larger gradient norm), conversion of the requests at time 0 contrasts less across the two runs. This motivates examining how responsiveness evolves as the student learns.

First, we note that live accessibility changes with both the request BtB_{t} and the kernel KtK_{t}, for instance, in a healthy run, BtB_{t} can deplete learnable components and rotate away from the student’s tangent map. To isolate kernel motion and how accessibility changes, we freeze each teacher’s initial field B0B_{0}, prefix bank, and token coordinates, then reapply the same request field at every checkpoint22 2 Time-00 request field is the least confounded as the initial student is the same in both the healthy and stalled runs. In practice, any representative probe bank of prefixes can be used to examine, for instance, the conversion health of more specific reasoning behaviors.. The common initialization anchors both fields to the same student, while preserving their distinct request profiles we saw earlier with the different teachers. With b0​(s)=B0​(s)/‖B0​(s)‖b_{0}(s)=B_{0}(s)/\|B_{0}(s)\|, at​(s)=b0​(s)⊤​Kt​(s,s)​b0​(s)=∑jλj,t​(s)​|vj,t​(s)⊤​b0​(s)|2.a_{t}(s)=b_{0}(s)^{\top}K_{t}(s,s)b_{0}(s)=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j,t}(s)|v_{j,t}(s)^{\top}b_{0}(s)|^{2}. Here (λj,t,vj,t)(\lambda_{j,t},v_{j,t}) are eigenpairs (eigenvalues and eigenvectors) of the self-kernel Kt​(s,s)K_{t}(s,s), and the request-energy-weighted average of at​(s)a_{t}(s) is At​[B0]A_{t}[B_{0}]. Larger eigenvalues amplify accessible directions; turning strong eigendirections toward B0B_{0} makes more of the same request visible. Both can increase local responsiveness (Section C.4).

At 1.5B in the healthy run, leading-subspace overlap falls to 0.770.77 by step 50 while leading strength remains near its initial value (Figure 4(b)). This means its eigenframe re-orients towards the request field in the early phase of training with nearly no scaling-amplification in the leading eigenvectors: the fixed request gains a median 5.55.5 percentage points of top-three projection, and its paired gain exceeds the other teacher’s by 1.791.79 points (Figure 4(c)). By step 200, leading eigenvalue strength reaches 2.31×2.31\times and median request-direction sensitivity 2.08×2.08\times the baseline. In contrast, the stalled run contracts in leading eigenvalue strengths and sensitivity (0.67×0.67\times and 0.83×0.83\times respectively). At 7B in the healthy run, eigenvector rotation is much less pronounced and adaptation is primarily amplification of the existing eigenframe: leading strength reaches 1.25×1.25\times with overlap 0.960.96 against the initial frame, while stalled leading strength falls to 0.74×0.74\times.

These results distinguish healthy and stalled pairings early on in an OPD training run in the requests they receive and the responsiveness their tangent geometry develop, giving diagnostics beyond the standard gradient norm and training loss from the request-conversion aspect. The next sub-section will study what comes next: when there is significant policy motion, cumulated over time, where do they head to? Why do two student models OPD-trained under the same teacher, both reducing training loss substantially, have different generalization performance under OPD?

3.3 Broadcast: why local agreement need not improve reasoning

Under JustRL-1.5B, both DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct substantially reduce their training loss. Yet DeepSeek gains accuracy (Section 3.2), while the base Qwen 1.5B model declines substantially on MATH within 100 steps. Why does learning from the same teacher help one learner and harm the other?

How do OPD updates change a per-prefix readout function?

Let us first examine how an OPD update influences a local, per-prefix readout function of a rollout, such as the training loss or entropy. It acts on two coupled axes: it changes which prefixes are encountered in future rollouts from the model, and it changes the model’s predictions at a fixed prefix.

More precisely, let us define a local prefix readout Yt​(x)Y_{t}(x). Define JY​(t)=𝔼νt​Yt​(x)J_{Y}(t)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}Y_{t}(x), where νt\nu_{t} is the observed prefix population. Then its rate of change (due to the parameter update) decomposes into “routing” and “drift”:

J˙Y(t)=∑xν˙t​(x)​Yt​(x)⏟RY​(t):routing+𝔼νt​Y˙t​(x)⏟DY​(t):drift,JY(b)−JY(a)=∫ab(RY+DY)dt.\dot{J}_{Y}(t)=\underbrace{\sum_{x}\dot{\nu}_{t}(x)Y_{t}(x)}_{R_{Y}(t):\ \text{routing}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}\dot{Y}_{t}(x)}_{D_{Y}(t):\ \text{drift}},\qquad J_{Y}(b)-J_{Y}(a)=\int_{a}^{b}(R_{Y}+D_{Y})\,dt. (5)

Drift changes the local, per-prefix readout over the current training population, while routing changes the probability weight assigned to the current prefixes, that is, which prefixes get exposed to teacher supervision in future updates.

At the more fundamental level of OPD’s dynamics, both of these channels are projections of the KK-Γ\Gamma broadcasts. The distinction is where the same update broadcasts. Recall from the response law that the weighted request population Γt\Gamma_{t} propagate through KtK_{t} to induce a logit response vt​(x)v_{t}(x) at every receiver prefix xx. With a temperature-τ\tau sampler, receiver xx and prediction token aa, this gives token log-probability velocity

ζt​(x,a)=∂tlog⁡πt​(a∣x)=(ea−πt(⋅∣x))⊤vt(x)τ,vt​(x)=∑sKt​(x,s)​Γt​(s).\zeta_{t}(x,a)=\partial_{t}\log\pi_{t}(a\mid x)=\frac{(e_{a}-\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid x))^{\top}v_{t}(x)}{\tau},\qquad v_{t}(x)=\sum_{s}K_{t}(x,s)\Gamma_{t}(s). (6)

At the observed prefix xx itself, vt​(x)v_{t}(x) changes its prediction, giving drift DY=𝔼νt​[∇zYt​(x)⊤​vt​(x)]D_{Y}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}[\nabla_{z}Y_{t}(x)^{\top}v_{t}(x)]. To reach that prefix, however, the autoregressive model must first generate its ancestor tokens, which also are the receivers of the KK-Γ\Gamma broadcast. Summing the log-probability velocity of the ancestor tokens gives the velocity of reach-probability of prefix xx, λt​(x)=∑j<h⁡(x)ζt​(xj,aj)\lambda_{t}(x)=\sum_{j<h(x)}\zeta_{t}(x_{j},a_{j}). This gives routing RY=Covνt⁡(Yt,λt)R_{Y}=\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{t}}(Y_{t},\lambda_{t}). Furthermore, the prefix visitation change causes the future training prefix distribution μ\mu to change: within any time interval [a,b][a,b],

μb(s)∝μa(s)eΛa:b(s),Λa:b(s)=∫abλt(s)dt→Γb=μbBb.\mu_{b}(s)\propto\mu_{a}(s)e^{\Lambda_{a:b}(s)},\qquad\Lambda_{a:b}(s)=\int_{a}^{b}\lambda_{t}(s)\,dt\;\;\rightarrow\;\Gamma_{b}=\mu_{b}B_{b}. (7)

The new rollouts (i.e. visited prefixes) supply the next requests and the induced Γ\Gamma field, on which the new round of updates and broadcasts are made.

Intuitively, significant prefix-visitation change can be either beneficial or damaging. For a weak student, it can route into low-quality, chaotic rollout distributions on which the teacher struggle to give requests that can help recover (or raise) the student’s intermediate reasoning performance and terminal scores. On the flip side, the continually refreshed training rollouts also allow the possibility of “online corrections”, where problematic reasoning behaviors broadcasted from early training can be corrected by the teacher mid-training. We will see these effects in our empirical analysis later.

To empirically study the effects of routing and drift in influencing the local readouts, we estimate their effects by cross-scoring training rollout banks and learners at time intervals. Write Mi​j=𝔼x∼νi​Yj​(x)M_{ij}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\nu_{i}}Y_{j}(x) for the average readout of learner jj on the frozen bank of rollouts extracted at time step ii, with i,j∈{a,b}i,j\in\{a,b\}. Replacing the bank at a fixed learner checkpoint measures routing; replacing the checkpoint on a fixed bank measures drift. Averaging the two replacement orders gives

R^a:b=12[(Mb​a−Ma​a)+(Mb​b−Ma​b)],D^a:b=12[(Ma​b−Ma​a)+(Mb​b−Mb​a)].\widehat{R}_{a:b}=\tfrac{1}{2}[(M_{ba}-M_{aa})+(M_{bb}-M_{ab})],\qquad\widehat{D}_{a:b}=\tfrac{1}{2}[(M_{ab}-M_{aa})+(M_{bb}-M_{ba})]. (8)

These contributions sum exactly to Mb​b−Ma​aM_{bb}-M_{aa}. Our curves accumulate them over consecutive windows; its relation to the path integrals and further details are in Sections C.7 and E.133 3 While a step-wise estimate for routing and drift is theoretically recommended, it is too expensive for our setting, and we resort to intervals of 20 update steps..

From local readouts to rollout-outcome readouts.

So far we have discussed how the KK-Γ\Gamma broadcasts change the model’s predictions per prefix, how they accumulate along ancestor tokens to change prefix visitation, and how they influence a local per-prefix readout function. Correctness, by contrast, is non-local, and known only after completing the full rollout, so its JYJ_{Y} expression must consider how “aligned” the policy motion is with terminal score when cumulated along a rollout trajectory.

Generally, given a trajectory-determined terminal readout function YY, set JY=𝔼Πt​YJ_{Y}=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi_{t}}Y and use the student’s continuation values QtY(x,a)=𝔼t[Y∣x,a]Q_{t}^{Y}(x,a)=\mathbb{E}_{t}[Y\mid x,a] and VtY​(x)=𝔼a∼πt​QtY​(x,a)V_{t}^{Y}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{t}}Q_{t}^{Y}(x,a). We obtain:

JY​(T)−JY​(t⋆)\displaystyle J_{Y}(T)-J_{Y}(t_{\star}) =∫t⋆T∑xdt​(x)​𝔼a∼πt​[ζt​(x,a)​(QtY​(x,a)−VtY​(x))⏟continuation advantage]​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{t_{\star}}^{T}\sum_{x}d_{t}(x)\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{t}}\!\left[\zeta_{t}(x,a)\underbrace{(Q_{t}^{Y}(x,a)-V_{t}^{Y}(x))}_{\text{continuation advantage}}\right]dt (9)
=1τ​∫t⋆T∑x,sdt​(x)​[πt⊙(QtY−VtY)]​(x)⊤​Kt​(x,s)​Γt​(s)​dt,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\tau}\int_{t_{\star}}^{T}\sum_{x,s}d_{t}(x)[\pi_{t}\odot(Q_{t}^{Y}-V_{t}^{Y})](x)^{\top}K_{t}(x,s)\Gamma_{t}(s)\,dt,

where dt​(x)d_{t}(x) is the probability of reaching xx. This weights motion by what the student can achieve. When the favored alternatives have similarly unsuccessful continuations, fitting their next-token distributions can yield little accuracy progress overall (see Section C.8 for the proof).

Weak 1.5B Qwen: routing into unreliable reasoning, then fitting uncertain supervision.

In the early phase of training, the teacher pushes the weak learner toward longer rollouts (such as heavy negative requests on the student’s “overly early” answer commitments), but these extensions become high-entropy and incoherent. The teacher supervision there also becomes much less concentrated than in the shallower rollout windows (Figure 5c,d). As seen in Figure 5(a) and (b), from step 1 to 20, loss rises 0.58→0.850.58\to 0.85 (routing +0.455+0.455 outweighs drift −0.187-0.187); entropy also rises mainly through routing. Intuitively, the student, which has never been trained to emit long reasoning rollouts, gets pushed into reasoning for long before committing an answer, and executing reasoning states which it is highly unfamiliar with. The teacher, conditioned on these low-quality states, also give much less confident guidance. The drift of the loss is small in this phase, however: the student has not learned the flatter prediction patterns of the teacher (uniformly) across the visited prefixes yet.

What happens after the initial routing-dominated phase is dominated by drift (local fitting) on the unreliable request distributions. As seen in Figure 5, entropy remains high within the band around 2−42-4 nats, and loss reduction is increasingly driven by drift, that is, the student is indeed fitting the teacher’s low confidence predictions on the chaotic, low-quality prefixes continually generated during training. To further test this, we find that, on the same batch-41 training prefixes, loss falls 0.79→0.060.79\to 0.06 while entropy falls 4.99→3.994.99\to 3.99: drift over the course of training actually broadcasts and sharpens predictions on this rollout bank toward an uncertain but slightly less entropic teacher (Sections C.9 and E.3.1).

Policy motion and the shifting value of continuations.

So far we see that the weak Qwen model’s failed run has the OPD update loop spending later, more “stable” drift-dominated updates learning from unreliable requests on the low-quality generative distribution. This helps us better understand how the training loss declines. Intuitively, fitting unreliable teacher supervision on high-entropy rollouts already suggests that this will not yield a better-reasoning student model. To understand how and why this process worsens terminal score more precisely, we need to turn to Equation 9: policy motion influences non-local readouts (including terminal score) through the value / advantage of the student’s continuations (namely the Q−VQ-V advantage summed across the prefixes), which can be in conflict with local teacher agreement.

While it is prohibitively expensive to directly compute the “velocity×\timesadvantage” term in Equation 9, we find on select banks of probing rollouts and continuations that as training proceeds, the model increasingly make local decisions whose continuation correctness decline, and complementarily, visit prefixes that are difficult to reach the right answer at increasingly shallower depth. This tells us that the per-token policy velocity of the model tend to align with “negative advantage” over the course of training, resulting in the overall decline of terminal accuracy. We elaborate on these studies below.

First, to probe the continuation-value term in Equation 9, we freeze a set of answer-decision prefixes from the initial student’s held-out MATH rollouts and intervene on the local “answer-versus-continue” decision token position. The student’s probability of the answer branch falls from 0.74→0.19→0.070.74\to 0.19\to 0.07 at steps 0, 20, 100, below the teacher’s 0.300.30 on the same prefixes. At update 20, while “routing” is dominating, counterfactual continuations from the two branches have similar downstream value (correct 0.300.30 for the “answer” branch and 0.290.29 for the “continue” branch), i.e. the student still maintains reasonable answer-reaching abilities. By update 100, however, the continue-branch rarely produces the answer (8%8\% of continuations). The teacher’s own continuations from the same prefixes is correct 0.600.60 of the time, which is much higher, so the gap is in the student’s degraded execution of the action branch, not in the branch itself. For a complete treatment of how we decompose and estimate Equation 9 see Section E.4.

Now, these probes fix the prefixes and probe how the student checkpoints continues them. As we discussed before, the broadcast mechanism changes both prefix visitation and continuations from them, therefore we next ask the complementary question of whether the prefixes visited during OPD also become increasingly harder to complete. We fix a few rollout depths and student checkpoints, sample prefixes generated from these checkpoints at those depths, and then let the initial student (as a reference policy) to finish. Keeping the continuer fixed makes changes in success reflect changes in prefix visitation. To understand the principled connections between these reference-continuer effects and Equation 9, please refer to Section E.7. Empirically, Figure 6 shows a clear increase in continuation difficulty due to the prefix visitation shift, on the axes of rollout depths and training length. At step 50, while the shallow prefixes remains usable (even slightly better than the initial policy’s own prefixes), it already yields less successful continuations on deep prefixes. As training goes on, the decline show up at increasingly shallower cuts of the rollout.

DeepSeek: stable learning acquiring epistemic behaviors.

DeepSeek supplies the clean contrast. Loss falls 0.263→0.0150.263\to 0.015, mainly through drift (−0.214-0.214) rather than routing (−0.033-0.033), indicating more more stable prefix visitations and local learning of requests. Furthermore, motivated by the epistemic-control request distribution found in Section 3.2, we design a local readout to examine the dynamics of how the model acquires intermediate reasoning behaviors, focusing on “wait”-family initiation at sentence starts (observed to initiate important backtracking and checking behaviors in R1-styled models (Marjanovic et al., 2026)). On each prefix, let wtw_{t} and qWq_{W} denote student and teacher WAIT-family probabilities. We freeze two classes: over-use (w0>qWw_{0}>q_{W}) and under-use (w0<qWw_{0}<q_{W}), and set the local readout to be log⁡[wt/(1−wt)]\log[w_{t}/(1-w_{t})] (log-odds of “wait” initiation).

Figure 7 plots cumulative routing and drift of the “wait”-readout. Filled circles move downward: drift suppresses initial over-use. Open triangles move upward: drift promotes initial under-use. The corresponding net changes are −1.82-1.82 and +1.92+1.92 nats. While there are short overshoots of routing-dominated changes (early false suppression of under-use positions and promotion of over-use positions), they are quickly stabilized. Moreover, teacher-relative disagreement also decreases on frozen and held-out rollout banks (Section E.2). Thus, unlike the failed learner’s case where drift-dominated reduction of training loss happened on unreliable prefixes, DeepSeek’s stabler drift-dominated reduction on training loss not only improves on its terminal score, but is accompanied by improvements in intermediate reasoning behaviors, with it sustaining prefix populations that allows to learn when to initiate a “wait”-based check as a representative example.

Preparation permits a different trajectory.

The base Qwen model, prepared with offline distillation training on teacher rollouts, also undergoes substantial prefix visitation shifts, but sustains useful learning. Unlike DeepSeek’s smoother refinement, its loss and checking behavior are nonmonotone: a routing-dominated overshoot in loss and reasoning (epistemic) behaviors are followed by lower-entropy rollouts and conditional moderation of reasoning behaviors dominated by drift. Its held-out gains suggest that a stronger starting policy with higher prefix quality and continuation-readiness makes these excursions amenable to correction. Full analysis in Section E.5.

3.4 Preparation: improving the starting point of on-policy learning

Section 3.3 suggests a direct intervention. As we saw in the last sub-section, OPD can fail because early policy changes route the weak student model into reasoning states it cannot yet execute reliably, and the training run spends a large chunk of time fitting unreliable requests on increasingly lower-quality prefixes. Then, a natural candidate intervention is that, before OPD, we force the student to visit higher-quality prefixes from the teacher itself and learn the teacher’s stronger continuations on those prefix populations. This suggests offline distillation to prepare the student model’s continuation abilities before running OPD, which can then expose finer student errors to the teacher and sustain more stable learning trajectory for online corrections when OPD changes prefix visitation, without the requests looking so foreign to the student in the OPD phase that it routes into irrecoverable rollout distributions.

We prepare with student/teacher pairings Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct/JustRL-1.5B (Qwen et al., 2025; He et al., 2025), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/AceReason-Nemotron-7B (Chen et al., 2025), and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct/Llama-3.1-Nemotron-Nano-8B-v1 (Llama Team, 2024; Bercovich et al., 2025), with students trained on their teachers’ solutions to OpenMathInstruct-2 (Toshniwal et al., 2024). We then compare OPD with continued offline distillation on the same DAPO-Math-17k prompt blocks (Yu et al., 2025), matching optimizer steps and sequence presentations.

Figure 8 shows higher pooled pass@kk accuracy for OPD than offline training through k=32k=32, using 32 responses per problem. The gains extend beyond pass@1 to sampled coverage and the distribution of per-problem solve rates. The reliability improvement is especially interesting: looking at pass@kk alone might give us the impression that OPD just solves more problems by rare chances, however, we find that OPD with appropriate preparation also enhances the per-problem solve rates for the models beyond the offline-distillation-only alternatives. Additionally, the preparation “dose study” (Figure 8, right) shows increasing value of offline-preparation for the later OPD phase. At 1.5B, one to four passes leaves the starting strict MATH pass@1 at 45.745.7–47.1%47.1\%, but raises the 100-step OPD endpoint from 45.9%45.9\% to 56.2%56.2\%. Similar trends are observed at 7B (Section F.2). Please refer to Section F.1 for further details.

4 Conclusion

Findings. We studied on-policy distillation as a feedback loop between teacher supervision, student response, and the rollout distribution that supplies future supervision. Our analysis separates two mechanisms in this loop: conversion, and broadcast. Across our settings, these mechanisms explain both stalled transfer and deterioration despite improving local teacher agreement. Offline preparation changes the starting point of this loop: even with little immediate accuracy improvement, it can enable substantial gains from subsequent OPD.

Limitations and discussion. Our empirical analysis is confined to mathematical reasoning and a select set of LLM models due to resource limitations. We also present a more detailed Q&A in Appendix A to further clarify potential ambiguities in our work.

Appendix A Mechanistic interpretation and key questions

Q1. What do the response law and decompositions in Sections 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 explain beyond their familiar mathematical ingredients?

They provide a connected mechanistic account of how dense local supervision can produce either weak transfer or deteriorating generation. OPD updates the policy that generates its next training population. Understanding its dynamics therefore requires following supervision beyond the current loss, through its effects on future behavior and training histories (student’s rollouts and the induced supervision signals / request field).

The theory separates three links in this process. First, Section 3.2 explains how a teacher’s requests become parameter motion: accessibility determines their expression through the student’s tangent map, while coherence determines how the resulting gradients combine. Teacher benchmark performance, magnitude of (KL-based) disagreement, or gradient norm alone cannot characterize this conversion. Second, Section 3.3 distinguishes changing a prediction from changing the ancestral decisions that make its history likely. Shared-parameter broadcast can increase exposure to a continuation without making the student better at executing it; the resulting histories then change the supervision received from the same fixed teacher. Third, Equation 9 connects the delivered response to completed outcomes through what the student’s remaining policy can achieve, separating teacher matching from useful reasoning.

Together, these links explain the structure of the empirical puzzles. The stronger-teacher study exposes the importance of gradient coherence and tangent accessibility; the degenerate run exposes that, under substantial policy motion, the degree of freedom granted to the learner to generate its own rollouts (training histories) can make it generate the new rollouts (reasoning states) which it has difficulty managing and grows uncertain on, inducing poorer-quality supervision signals. Loss reduction dominated by local fitting on these poorly supervised rollouts cannot improve the learner’s terminal scores. The mechanisms revealed in the degenerate run motivates preparing the student for the continuations that OPD will elicit, even when preparation does not substantially improve current accuracy by itself. The theoretical contribution is the integrated explanation that makes these mechanisms distinguishable, connects them to outcomes, and motivates an intervention that boosts the model’s learning stability and generalization.

Q2. Why is every training run reported with a single seed?

Cost. The runs behind this paper were trained and evaluated on GH200 nodes, and the single-seed set already consumed roughly 4,000 GPU-hours, which is at the limit of our computing resources. OPD is known to be computationally demanding, we therefore designed the experiments so that the main comparisons do not rest on seed variance. The mechanism measurements of Sections 3.2 and 3.3 are exact identities evaluated within a run, on fixed receiver banks and fixed checkpoints, and their uncertainty is reported at the level of problems or sites (paired bootstrap intervals). The outcome comparisons of Section 3.4 are paired within a student-teacher pair on the same problems and replicated across three pairs and two student scales. What single seeds leave unquantified is run-to-run variation of the training trajectories themselves.

Q3. Why does Section 3.3 need both prefix-level routing/drift (Equation 5) and trajectory-level continuation advantages (Equation 9) to explain degeneration?

For loss or entropy, JY=𝔼νt​Yt​(x)J_{Y}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}Y_{t}(x) describes predictions on the currently observed histories. Cross-scoring separates changes in those histories from changes in predictions on the same histories. In Figure 5, the initial student is already highly uncertain on the deep histories that later become prevalent, while subsequent fitting sharpens them. On identical batch-41 histories, discrepancy falls 0.79→0.060.79\to 0.06 and entropy 4.99→3.994.99\to 3.99. Together with the stopping/reach probes, these measurements distinguish routing followed by fitting from uniform entropy-increasing drift (Sections E.3 and E.3.1).

But fitting a prefix and improving the completion from it are different effects. For terminal correctness, JY=𝔼Πt​YJ_{Y}=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi_{t}}Y, and the conditional value VtY​(x)V_{t}^{Y}(x) depends on every downstream decision. At an intermediate cut of the autoregressive trace, its derivative separates changes in reaching the cut from changes in the remaining policy. Unrolling the latter gives the continuation-advantage weighting in Equation 9; replacing it with a derivative of the logits at xx alone would omit downstream effects (Section C.8). Thus, a teacher-preferred next token need not help if the student cannot complete the reasoning it initiates. The prefix analysis establishes the observed routing-then-fitting pattern; the outcome analysis explains why local fitting need not restore correctness. Entropy enters the argument only as a prefix-level readout.

Q4. Could the responsiveness changes in Section 3.2 (Figure 4) simply reflect changing teacher–student disagreement or generic kernel movement?

A live accessibility measure At​[Bt]A_{t}[B_{t}] can change because either the requests or the kernel change. We therefore fix the initial numerical requests B0B_{0}, exact histories, and output coordinates across checkpoints. Since only the kernel varies in At​[B0]A_{t}[B_{0}], its change measures responsiveness to the same supervision (Section C.4).

To test whether eigenspace movement reflects teacher-specific adaptation, we evaluate both teachers’ frozen fields in the same checkpoint kernel and compare their projection gains, separating preferential reorientation from shared movement that benefits both fields. Healthy 1.5B exhibits preferential reorientation; healthy 7B mainly amplifies existing directions; stalled runs lose sensitivity to the fixed requests (Section D.5). These findings complement the initial accessibility/coherence decomposition, which exposes conversion differences concealed by comparable gradient norms across the runs.

Q5. What does preparation in Sections 3.4 and 8 contribute beyond offline warm-up, and how does Section 3.3 motivate it?

The contribution is an explanation of why the value of a warm-up stage, already used in prior work (Appendix B), should be assessed through subsequent learning. The failure mechanism identifies a mismatch between making extended reasoning likely and being able to execute it. Offline distillation supplies teacher-generated reasoning histories without requiring the initial student to generate them first. It can therefore prepare continuation skills and reasoning-state management that become useful as OPD changes visitation: continuation readiness, a benefit beyond higher starting accuracy – our pass@k results clearly demonstrate this.

Appendix B Expanded related work

B.1 Core related works

Distillation and the OPD loop. Knowledge distillation transfers teacher outputs (Hinton et al., 2015), including teacher-generated sequences (Kim and Rush, 2016). DAgger, the seminal online imitation algorithm, addresses distribution shift through expert feedback on learner-visited states (Ross et al., 2011); Lin et al. (2020) develop this connection for autoregressive distillation. MiniLLM uses reverse KL and student-generated samples (Gu et al., 2024), (Agarwal et al., 2024; Piskorz et al., 2026) study the choice of divergence loss, and Lu and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) demonstrate practical OPD for reasoning and personalization. These methods motivate our question: how does dense supervision on student histories produce successful transfer, stagnation, or degeneration? We develop a systematic first-principles account of the coupled loop through which shared-parameter updates change predictions, renew visited histories, and reshape subsequent supervision.

Kernel response laws. The neural tangent kernel connects parameter learning to function-space change (Jacot et al., 2018). Malladi et al. (2023) analyze language-model finetuning through kernels, including an Adam extension; Ren and Sutherland (2025) decompose prediction changes through normalization, empirical-kernel, and loss-gradient terms for SFT and preference finetuning, including offline DPO. Tomihari (2026) studies update propagation in RL post-training. OPD needs different theoretical and empirical machinery for two reasons. Its on-policy sampling moves the learning distribution itself, so the analysis must track this motion, which is absent from the offline algorithms (SFT and offline DPO) studied by Ren and Sutherland (2025). Its supervision is also dense and token-level and can be disconnected from the reasoning outcome (such as accuracy), whereas RL gives only sparse, outcome-level learning signals.

Nevertheless, the fundamental response law of the shared-parameter neural learner is shared with Ren and Sutherland (2025). We then follow the induced motion through the rest of the OPD loop: changes at ancestor decisions alter reach probabilities, renew the training source, and thereby change the requests driving future updates. Combining the evolving kernel, routing/drift split, and continuation-value analysis yields a mechanistic account of how optimization changes future supervision and outcomes (Sections 3 and C).

Cumulative weight geometry vs the geometry of request conversion. Shen et al. (2026) find low stable rank and early stabilization of dominant subspaces in cumulative weight-matrix changes; constrained-training experiments test those subspaces’ functional sufficiency. We instead analyze the current logit Jacobian and the response it delivers to specified teacher requests. The Jacobian can change even when cumulative displacement is low-rank. Frozen histories, coordinates, and requests isolate amplification and reorientation; crossed teacher fields test preferential adaptation in the same kernel (Sections C.4 and D.5). Distinguishing local accessibility from collective coherence further explains why individually expressible requests can cancel. These analyses concern how geometry enables or obstructs transfer.

Local fitting vs task performance. Policy-gradient theory (Sutton et al., 1999) and cost-to-go-aware imitation learning (Ross and Bagnell, 2014) connect actions to subsequent outcomes. G-OPD interprets distillation through KL-constrained RL and reward extrapolation (Yang et al., 2026). Armandpour et al. (2026) use student continuation-success probabilities to derive an ideal local logit direction and measure its alignment with distillation signals (however, they acknowledge that such estimations in long-CoT reasoning can be very noisy). Uemura and Suzuki (2026) theoretically studies the dynamics of self-distillation for a single-layer neural network, and analyzes how the supervision affects long-horizon traversal of directed acyclic graphs, invoking tools such as future advantage in their analysis. Our analysis connects this type of outcome perspective to delivered motion: ∑sKt​(x,s)​Γt​(s)\sum_{s}K_{t}(x,s)\Gamma_{t}(s) includes the effects of all coupled source prefixes in addition to the request at xx. Crucially, prefix readouts 𝔼νt​Yt​(x)\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}Y_{t}(x) and terminal outcomes 𝔼Πt​Y\mathbb{E}_{\Pi_{t}}Y are different objects. At an intermediate cut-position in the autoregressive rollout, terminal change splits into the change in reaching that prefix and the change in the continuations; unrolling the latter and recombining both terms yields the advantage-weighted contribution of every decision (Equations 9 and C.8). This separates reaching a prefix, fitting there, and completing it successfully –the distinction underlying the degeneration mechanism and continuation readiness.

Degeneration involves source feedback as well as supervision quality. Fu et al. (2026) study unreliable supervision and implementation choices; Jin et al. (2026a) augment high-entropy teacher supervision with forward KL; and Zhu et al. (2026) analyze signals induced by top-KK truncation, renormalization, and stop-gradient conventions. Li et al. (2026b) also observe deterioration with prefix depth. Contemporaneous work by Wang et al. (2026) studies teacher mismatch and length exploitation. Our first-principled analysis reveals a phased failure mechanism: early routing makes already-uncertain continuations prevalent, after which substantial fitting can sharpen those very histories without restoring useful generation (Sections E.3 and E.3.1). Our routing-drift machinery, coupled with the learning-value decomposition (for terminal-accuracy readout) distinguish the failure mechanism from a naive, uniform entropy-increasing learning process. The important feedback is that the histories made common by earlier updates become the source of later supervision. The prepared learner’s different trajectory further shows why source movement itself is not synonymous with failure, and its continuation-readiness helps in exposing useful subsequent learning.

Offline preparation can improve readiness for learning without improving immediate accuracy. Li et al. (2026b) motivate cold-start SFT by reducing thinking-pattern mismatch and improving overlap. Their §5.1/Figure 8 studies a strong standalone-SFT regime: the SFT initialization already exceeds the direct-OPD endpoint on all three plotted benchmarks, with little further gains from OPD. We study a different regime, where the student-teacher gap is significant, and preparation leaves starting accuracy near the unprepared student’s but changes subsequent OPD from deterioration to substantial improvement. The principled motivation is continuation readiness: the outcome analysis and observed failure mechanisms in Section 3.3 identify a distinction between increasing a history’s reach and executing its continuation successfully. Teacher-generated trajectories provide training on such histories before the student must reach them itself. Our dose study exposes deferred benefits and a sharply nonmonotonic stability pattern at 7B; the prepared-run analysis traces a different subsequent routing/fitting process (Tables 14 and E.5).

In contemporaneous work Simple-OPD (Liu et al., 2026) studies warm-up data, duration, and LoRA parameterization, including benefits from incorrect teacher-compatible traces and differences between SFT and downstream rankings. These findings complement our mechanistic account linking preparation to source feedback and continuation values. The key result is an altered learning trajectory; the preparation dose-response experiments demonstrate this interesting benefit.

B.2 More related works

Reasoning interpretability. Part of the focus of our work is on how LLMs learn to reason (from a teacher model), and our analysis methodology is partly inspired by the discoveries in the reasoning interpretability community. Venhoff et al. (2025a) is especially relevant, as they discovered that RL-trained models tend to acquire the ability to manage “when” to fire a reasoning mechanism (be it an “epistemic control” mechanism such as backtracking or planning, or computation mechanisms like estimating an inequality); Marjanovic et al. (2026) directly studies the chain-of-thought reasoning mechanisms of DeepSeek-R1 models, which our DeepSeek student models are distilled from, also inspiring our analysis on the epistemic control transmission in OPD. More broadly, Bogdan et al. (2025); Baek and Tegmark (2025); Venhoff et al. (2025b); Troitskii et al. (2025); Hong et al. (2025); Ward et al. (2025) identify causal mechanisms behind LLMs’ reasoning behaviors in logic, mathematics and other related domains.

OPD and its variants. On-policy distillation is becoming increasingly popular in industry post-training pipelines (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026). Many variants are being proposed, including selecting which tokens to perform supervision on (Jin et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2026), and curriculum-styled variants (Ziheng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). The survey on OPD Song and Zheng (2026b) is also a good reference for understanding the research landscape in this area.

Learning dynamics. Many classic works lie in this space and are predecessors to recent studies of LLM learning dynamics. Biehl and Schwarze (1995); Saad and Solla (1995); Saxe et al. (2014); Goldt et al. (2019) are early representative works, studying how learning trajectories and generalization depend on the model, initialization, and training process, and providing foundations for our analysis of how teacher supervision changes the student over time. Furthermore, a particular line of work study feature learning in nonlinear neural networks: Baratin et al. (2021); Atanasov et al. (2022); Hong et al. (2024); Allen-Zhu and Li (2022); Allen-Zhu and Li (2023a) study how the nonlinear neural network’s geometry evolves and aligns with the task, showing feature re-orientation early on in (pre-)training that precedes appreciable loss reduction (sometimes called the “lottery winning” phase, where certain neurons or features better align towards loss-reducing directions early in training without substantial loss-reduction yet). These works are especially relevant to our analysis of the student’s changing responsiveness to teacher requests in Section 3.2, and to offline preparation whose benefits become apparent through subsequent learning. Additionally, another relevant line of work in the pre-LLM era study dynamics of DNN distillation. Phuong and Lampert (2019); Ji and Zhu (2020); Hong et al. (2021); Allen-Zhu and Li (2023b); Panahi et al. (2022); He and Ozay (2022) examine how the geometry of the learning problem, teacher knowledge, and the student’s representation affect transfer, using linear, deep linear, or kernel-based analyses of the SGD-based learning trajectory.

This appendix follows Sections 2 and 3. It gives the assumptions and proofs for the main-text identities, then the specializations used to interpret the experiments.
