C.1 Setup: policies, requests, and standing assumptions

Connection to Section 2. We distinguish the model distribution, the sampling distribution, and the numerical field pulled back into parameter space. This distinction is needed for both the proofs and the experimental diagnostics.

Notation.

A prompt is denoted by bb, a source prefix by ss, and a receiver prefix by xx. A complete trajectory is ξ\xi; τ>0\tau>0 is reserved for sampling temperature. The integer kk indexes optimizer updates, jj indexes generated-token depth, and tt indexes continuous training time. All gradients of scalar functions are column vectors. The matrix Φθ​(x)∈ℝ|𝒱|×d\Phi_{\theta}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d} has row aa equal to ∇θzθ​(x,a)⊤\nabla_{\theta}z_{\theta}(x,a)^{\top}, so Kθ​(x,s)=Φθ​(x)​Φθ​(s)⊤K_{\theta}(x,s)=\Phi_{\theta}(x)\Phi_{\theta}(s)^{\top}. We write 𝖠p=I−𝟏​p⊤\mathsf{A}^{p}=I-\mathbf{1}p^{\top} for the log-softmax normalization matrix, AA for scalar accessibility, and 𝒜Y\mathcal{A}^{Y} for continuation advantage. A logit-space readout gradient is denoted by χ∈ℝ|𝒱|\chi\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}; its parameter-space pullback is ψ=Φ⊤​χ∈ℝd\psi=\Phi^{\top}\chi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Norms without a subscript are Euclidean. ∥⋅∥op\|\cdot\|_{\rm op} denotes the induced operator norm.

Assumption C.1 (Finite generation trees and regular parameter paths).

The prompt set ℬ\mathcal{B} and vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V} are finite, and generation has a finite cap HmaxH_{\max}. Each prefix contains its prompt and its full generated ancestry. Appending a token is deterministic. A node is terminal after a stopping token or at the cap, and has no further decisions. The terminal rule and chat template are fixed. The prompt distribution β\beta is fixed (and independent of model parameters); prompts of zero probability are omitted.

The parameter path θ:I→ℝd\theta:I\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, on a compact interval II, is continuous and piecewise C1C^{1} with finitely many pieces. For every prefix under consideration, zθ​(x)z_{\theta}(x) is C2C^{2} on an open neighborhood of the path and of any parameter segment used for a finite-step calculation. The model distribution is the full-vocabulary policy pθ=softmax⁡(zθ)p_{\theta}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{\theta}). The teacher qq is fixed and is positive on every coordinate used in an exact-KL calculation (which softmax-output models do satisfy).

For the sampling identities, each nonterminal prefix xx has a fixed nonempty allowed vocabulary set 𝒱π​(x)⊆𝒱\mathcal{V}_{\pi}(x)\subseteq\mathcal{V} and

πθ​(a∣x)=exp⁡(zθ​(x,a)/τ)∑c∈𝒱π​(x)exp⁡(zθ​(x,c)/τ)(a∈𝒱π​(x)),πθ​(a∣x)=0(a∉𝒱π​(x)).\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x)=\frac{\exp(z_{\theta}(x,a)/\tau)}{\sum_{c\in\mathcal{V}_{\pi}(x)}\exp(z_{\theta}(x,c)/\tau)}\quad(a\in\mathcal{V}_{\pi}(x)),\qquad\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x)=0\quad(a\notin\mathcal{V}_{\pi}(x)).

The temperature τ>0\tau>0, allowed sets, and any observation or source masks are fixed. The full-vocabulary sampler is the case 𝒱π​(x)=𝒱\mathcal{V}_{\pi}(x)=\mathcal{V}.

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the resulting finite sets of nonterminal and terminal prefixes. A trajectory ξ=(b,a0,…,aN−1)\xi=(b,a_{0},\ldots,a_{N-1}) ends at its first terminal node, with N≤HmaxN\leq H_{\max}, and has probability

Πt​(ξ)=β⁡(b)​∏j=0N−1πt​(aj∣xj).\Pi_{t}(\xi)=\beta(b)\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}\pi_{t}(a_{j}\mid x_{j}).

For any node xx, including a terminal node, dt​(x)d_{t}(x) is its reach-probability. It is the same product truncated at depth h⁡(x)h(x). On terminal nodes dt​(x)=Πt​(x)d_{t}(x)=\Pi_{t}(x); on nonterminal nodes the sum ∑xdt​(x)\sum_{x}d_{t}(x) is generally not one. Every allowed trajectory has positive probability. Finiteness and the stated regularity justify every interchange of sums and derivatives below. Identities for derivatives hold on each smooth piece, hence almost everywhere, and integrate across the entire interval. The results take the path as given and are independent of any existence or uniqueness theorem for an autonomous training flow.

The raw direction is

gt​(s)=Φt​(s)⊤​Bt​(s),ut=∑sμt​(s)​gt​(s),Γt​(s)=μt​(s)​Bt​(s).g_{t}(s)=\Phi_{t}(s)^{\top}B_{t}(s),\qquad u_{t}=\sum_{s}\mu_{t}(s)g_{t}(s),\qquad\Gamma_{t}(s)=\mu_{t}(s)B_{t}(s).

Here BtB_{t} is a declared numerical logit-space field. The specialization θ˙t=ut\dot{\theta}_{t}=u_{t} is called the raw flow. An actual optimizer path uses its realized θ˙t\dot{\theta}_{t}. Restricted diagnostic fields are extended by zero outside their recorded token coordinates, and their Jacobians are restricted consistently; these diagnostic supports leave the sampler’s allowed set unchanged.

Lemma C.2 (Log-softmax differentiation and centering).

Write π=πθ(⋅∣x)\pi=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) as a vector in the full vocabulary, with zeros outside its fixed allowed set, and let 𝖠π=I−𝟏​π⊤\mathsf{A}^{\pi}=I-\mathbf{1}\pi^{\top}. For each allowed token aa,

∇θ​log​πθ​(a∣x)=τ−1​Φθ​(x)⊤​(ea−π),∑aπ⁡(a∣x)​∇θ​log⁡π⁡(a∣x)=0.\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x)=\tau^{-1}\Phi_{\theta}(x)^{\top}(e_{a}-\pi),\qquad\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi(a\mid x)=0.

Consequently ζt​(x,a):=∂tlog⁡πt​(a∣x)\zeta_{t}(x,a):=\partial_{t}\log\pi_{t}(a\mid x) satisfies ∑aπt​(a∣x)​ζt​(x,a)=0\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid x)\zeta_{t}(x,a)=0. If 𝟏⊤​w=0\mathbf{1}^{\top}w=0, then (𝖠π)⊤​w=w(\mathsf{A}^{\pi})^{\top}w=w. Sums involving log⁡π\log\pi or ζ\zeta range only over allowed tokens.

Proof.

For allowed aa, the logarithm of the displayed sampler in Assumption C.1 is

logπ(a∣x)=τ−1z(x,a)−log∑c∈𝒱π​(x)exp(z(x,c)/τ).\log\pi(a\mid x)=\tau^{-1}z(x,a)-\log\sum_{c\in\mathcal{V}_{\pi}(x)}\exp(z(x,c)/\tau).

Its partial derivative with respect to any full-vocabulary logit z⁡(x,c)z(x,c) is τ−1(𝟏{a=c}−π(c∣x))\tau^{-1}(\mathbf{1}\{a=c\}-\pi(c\mid x)), including the value zero when cc is disallowed. The chain rule proves the gradient formula. Averaging over allowed aa yields

τ−1​Φ​(x)⊤​(∑aπ⁡(a∣x)​ea−π​∑aπ⁡(a∣x))=0.\tau^{-1}\Phi(x)^{\top}\left(\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)e_{a}-\pi\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid x)\right)=0.

Pairing this equality with θ˙t\dot{\theta}_{t} gives the zero-mean velocity. Finally, (𝖠π)⊤​w=(I−π​𝟏⊤)​w=w−π⁡(𝟏⊤​w)=w(\mathsf{A}^{\pi})^{\top}w=(I-\pi\mathbf{1}^{\top})w=w-\pi(\mathbf{1}^{\top}w)=w. ∎

Proposition C.3 (Exact reverse-KL request).

At a fixed prefix, let c=∑apa​log⁡(pa/qa)c=\sum_{a}p_{a}\log(p_{a}/q_{a}), ℓa=log⁡(pa/qa)\ell_{a}=\log(p_{a}/q_{a}), and ℓ¯=∑apa​ℓa\bar{\ell}=\sum_{a}p_{a}\ell_{a}, with p=softmax⁡(z)p=\mathrm{softmax}(z) and qa>0q_{a}>0. Then

Ba=−∂zac=pa(ℓ¯−ℓa),𝟏⊤B=0,g=Φ⊤B=−∇θc.B_{a}=-\partial_{z_{a}}c=p_{a}(\bar{\ell}-\ell_{a}),\qquad\mathbf{1}^{\top}B=0,\qquad g=\Phi^{\top}B=-\nabla_{\theta}c. (10)

For fixed source weights μ\mu, u=∑sμ⁡(s)​g​(s)u=\sum_{s}\mu(s)g(s) is the negative gradient of ∑sμ⁡(s)​c​(s)\sum_{s}\mu(s)c(s).

Proof.

Positivity makes the logarithms differentiable. Since ∂zapb=pb(𝟏{a=b}−pa)\partial_{z_{a}}p_{b}=p_{b}(\mathbf{1}\{a=b\}-p_{a}) and ∂pb[pb​log⁡(pb/qb)]=ℓb+1\partial_{p_{b}}[p_{b}\log(p_{b}/q_{b})]=\ell_{b}+1, we have

∂zac\displaystyle\partial_{z_{a}}c =∑bpb(𝟏{a=b}−pa)(ℓb+1)\displaystyle=\sum_{b}p_{b}(\mathbf{1}\{a=b\}-p_{a})(\ell_{b}+1)
=pa​(ℓa+1)−pa​∑bpb​(ℓb+1)=pa​(ℓa−ℓ¯).\displaystyle=p_{a}(\ell_{a}+1)-p_{a}\sum_{b}p_{b}(\ell_{b}+1)=p_{a}(\ell_{a}-\bar{\ell}).

Thus ∑aBa=ℓ¯​∑apa−∑apa​ℓa=0\sum_{a}B_{a}=\bar{\ell}\sum_{a}p_{a}-\sum_{a}p_{a}\ell_{a}=0. The chain rule gives ∇θc=Φ⊤​∇zc\nabla_{\theta}c=\Phi^{\top}\nabla_{z}c; linearity of the finite sum proves the last assertion when μ\mu is held fixed. ∎

This is a full-distribution identity. For an implemented objective, such as a truncated-support loss or detached-coefficient surrogate, BB must be that objective’s own complete numerical negative logit derivative, including the softmax coupling. For the conversion diagnostic, BB denotes the explicitly specified audit field in Section D.3. The response and conversion results hold for this field’s pullback, whether or not that pullback coincides with exact-KL descent. Holding μ\mu fixed applies to computing one update; subsequent source populations can change.

C.2 Response law: exact finite steps and controlled remainders

Connection to Section 3.1, Equation 2. The integral is exact for an arbitrary realized step. The main-text kernel expression is its raw-gradient, first-order specialization.

Proposition C.4 (Exact response and Taylor remainder).

Let Δ​θ=θk+1−θk\Delta\theta=\theta_{k+1}-\theta_{k}, and let θr=θk+r​Δ​θ\theta_{r}=\theta_{k}+r\Delta\theta for 0≤r≤10\leq r\leq 1. For any fixed receiver xx and token aa,

δkp​(x,a)=∫01∇θ​log​pθr​(a∣x)⊤​Δ​θ​𝑑r.\delta_{k}^{p}(x,a)=\int_{0}^{1}\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta_{r}}(a\mid x)^{\top}\Delta\theta\,dr. (11)

If Mk​(x,a)=sup0≤r≤1‖∇θ2​log⁡pθr​(a∣x)‖opM_{k}(x,a)=\sup_{0\leq r\leq 1}\|\nabla_{\theta}^{2}\log p_{\theta_{r}}(a\mid x)\|_{\rm op}, then

δkp​(x,a)=∇θ​log​pk​(a∣x)⊤​Δ​θ+Rk​(x,a),|Rk​(x,a)|≤12​Mk​(x,a)​‖Δ​θ‖2.\delta_{k}^{p}(x,a)=\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{k}(a\mid x)^{\top}\Delta\theta+R_{k}(x,a),\qquad|R_{k}(x,a)|\leq\tfrac{1}{2}M_{k}(x,a)\|\Delta\theta\|^{2}.

The corresponding exact logit displacement is zk+1​(x)−zk​(x)=∫01Φθr​(x)​Δ​θ​𝑑rz_{k+1}(x)-z_{k}(x)=\int_{0}^{1}\Phi_{\theta_{r}}(x)\Delta\theta\,dr.

Proof.

Define f⁡(r)=log⁡pθr​(a∣x)f(r)=\log p_{\theta_{r}}(a\mid x). Its first two derivatives are

f′​(r)=∇θ​log​pθr​(a∣x)⊤​Δ​θ,f′′​(r)=Δ​θ⊤​∇θ2​log​pθr​(a∣x)​Δ​θ.f^{\prime}(r)=\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta_{r}}(a\mid x)^{\top}\Delta\theta,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(r)=\Delta\theta^{\top}\nabla_{\theta}^{2}\log p_{\theta_{r}}(a\mid x)\Delta\theta.

The fundamental theorem of calculus gives Equation 11. Applying it also to f′f^{\prime} and changing the order of integration over 0≤v≤r≤10\leq v\leq r\leq 1 gives

f⁡(1)−f⁡(0)−f′​(0)=∫01∫0rf′′​(v)​𝑑v​𝑑r=∫01(1−v)​f′′​(v)​𝑑v.f(1)-f(0)-f^{\prime}(0)=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{r}f^{\prime\prime}(v)\,dv\,dr=\int_{0}^{1}(1-v)f^{\prime\prime}(v)\,dv.

The Hessian is continuous on a compact segment, so Mk​(x,a)<∞M_{k}(x,a)<\infty. The bound follows from |f′′​(v)|≤Mk​(x,a)​‖Δ​θ‖2|f^{\prime\prime}(v)|\leq M_{k}(x,a)\|\Delta\theta\|^{2} and ∫01(1−v)​𝑑v=1/2\int_{0}^{1}(1-v)\,dv=1/2. Applying the same first-derivative calculation to each logit proves the vector identity. ∎

Corollary C.5 (Small-step response law).

For Δ​θk=η​uk\Delta\theta_{k}=\eta u_{k} with uk=∑sμk​(s)​Φk​(s)⊤​Bk​(s)u_{k}=\sum_{s}\mu_{k}(s)\Phi_{k}(s)^{\top}B_{k}(s),

δkp​(x,a)=η​∑sμk​(s)​[𝖠kp​(x)​Kk​(x,s)​Bk​(s)]a+Rk​(x,a),|Rk​(x,a)|≤12​η2​Mk​(x,a)​‖uk‖2.\delta_{k}^{p}(x,a)=\eta\sum_{s}\mu_{k}(s)[\mathsf{A}_{k}^{p}(x)K_{k}(x,s)B_{k}(s)]_{a}+R_{k}(x,a),\qquad|R_{k}(x,a)|\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\eta^{2}M_{k}(x,a)\|u_{k}\|^{2}.

For fixed θk,uk\theta_{k},u_{k} and sufficiently small η\eta, the remainder is O⁡(η2)O(\eta^{2}), as in Equation 2.

Proof.

At temperature one, Lemma C.2 gives ∇θ​log​pk​(a∣x)⊤=ea⊤​𝖠kp​(x)​Φk​(x)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{k}(a\mid x)^{\top}=e_{a}^{\top}\mathsf{A}_{k}^{p}(x)\Phi_{k}(x). Substituting uku_{k} in Proposition C.4 therefore yields

∇θ​log​pk​(a∣x)⊤​uk=∑sμk​(s)​ea⊤​𝖠kp​(x)​Φk​(x)​Φk​(s)⊤​Bk​(s),\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{k}(a\mid x)^{\top}u_{k}=\sum_{s}\mu_{k}(s)e_{a}^{\top}\mathsf{A}_{k}^{p}(x)\Phi_{k}(x)\Phi_{k}(s)^{\top}B_{k}(s),

which is the asserted kernel term. The remainder bound follows by substituting Δ​θk=η​uk\Delta\theta_{k}=\eta u_{k}. To justify the asymptotic notation, choose η0>0\eta_{0}>0 so that all segments with |η|≤η0|\eta|\leq\eta_{0} lie in a compact neighborhood where the Hessian is continuous. Its supremum on this neighborhood supplies a single bound independent of η\eta. A family of varying directions requires a uniform bound on their norms as well. ∎

Velocity and the optimizer.

At every differentiable time on an actual parameter path,

vt(x):=z˙t(x)=Φt(x)θ˙t,ζt(x,a)=τ−1(ea−πt(⋅∣x))⊤vt(x).v_{t}(x):=\dot{z}_{t}(x)=\Phi_{t}(x)\dot{\theta}_{t},\qquad\zeta_{t}(x,a)=\tau^{-1}(e_{a}-\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid x))^{\top}v_{t}(x).

These follow directly by the chain rule and Lemma C.2. Under gradient flow, substituting θ˙t=ut\dot{\theta}_{t}=u_{t} gives vt​(x)=∑sKt​(x,s)​Γt​(s)v_{t}(x)=\sum_{s}K_{t}(x,s)\Gamma_{t}(s) and hence Equation 6. With momentum, preconditioning, clipping, or weight decay, the actual θ˙t\dot{\theta}_{t} in general differs from the raw utu_{t}. However, with the rich tradition of theoretical analysis on the learning dynamics of neural networks including the seminal Ren and Sutherland (2025); Jacot et al. (2018); Arora et al. (2019), gradient-flow analysis is still genuinely informative in obtaining rich theoretical insights. We leave extensions to the more convoluted optimizer settings to future work.

C.3 Collective response and its geometry

Connection to Section 3.2, Equations 3 and 4. We fix the checkpoint, output coordinates, and normalized bank ν\nu in this subsection. Zero-weight sites are omitted. The space ℋν\mathcal{H}_{\nu} of fields on the remaining finite bank has the inner product

⟨F,G⟩ν=∑sν⁡(s)​F​(s)⊤​G​(s),‖F‖ν2=⟨F,F⟩ν.\langle F,G\rangle_{\nu}=\sum_{s}\nu(s)F(s)^{\top}G(s),\qquad\|F\|_{\nu}^{2}=\langle F,F\rangle_{\nu}.

Define 𝒥:ℝd→ℋν\mathcal{J}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathcal{H}_{\nu} by (𝒥​v)​(s)=Φ​(s)​v(\mathcal{J}v)(s)=\Phi(s)v. This is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, so orthogonal projections and adjoints are well-defined.

Proposition C.6 (Collective response and conversion factorization).

Let g⁡(s)=Φ​(s)⊤​B​(s)g(s)=\Phi(s)^{\top}B(s), u=𝔼ν​gu=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}g, P=‖B‖ν2P=\|B\|_{\nu}^{2}, and Dg=𝔼ν​‖g‖2D_{g}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\|g\|^{2}. The adjoint is 𝒥∗​B=u\mathcal{J}^{*}B=u, and 𝒦=𝒥​𝒥∗\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{J}\mathcal{J}^{*} is self-adjoint and positive semidefinite. For the same-bank raw direction and P>0P>0,

z˙=𝒦​B=Ξ​B+r,Ξ=⟨B,𝒦​B⟩νP=‖u‖2P≥0,⟨B,r⟩ν=0.\dot{z}=\mathcal{K}B=\Xi B+r,\qquad\Xi=\frac{\langle B,\mathcal{K}B\rangle_{\nu}}{P}=\frac{\|u\|^{2}}{P}\geq 0,\qquad\langle B,r\rangle_{\nu}=0.

If also Dg>0D_{g}>0, then

A=DgP,C=‖u‖2Dg,Ξ=A​C,‖u‖2=P​A​C,0≤C≤1.A=\frac{D_{g}}{P},\qquad C=\frac{\|u\|^{2}}{D_{g}},\qquad\Xi=AC,\qquad\|u\|^{2}=PAC,\qquad 0\leq C\leq 1.

Here C=1C=1 exactly when g⁡(s)=ug(s)=u at every positive-weight site, and C=0C=0 exactly when u=0u=0. If P>0P>0 but Dg=0D_{g}=0, then u=0u=0, A=Ξ=0A=\Xi=0, and CC is undefined. If P=0P=0, then B=g=u=0B=g=u=0 on the bank and A,C,ΞA,C,\Xi are not defined by these ratios.

Proof.

For any field FF and parameter vector vv,

⟨F,𝒥​v⟩ν=∑sν⁡(s)​F​(s)⊤​Φ​(s)​v=(∑sν⁡(s)​Φ​(s)⊤​F​(s))⊤​v.\langle F,\mathcal{J}v\rangle_{\nu}=\sum_{s}\nu(s)F(s)^{\top}\Phi(s)v=\left(\sum_{s}\nu(s)\Phi(s)^{\top}F(s)\right)^{\top}v.

This proves the adjoint formula. It also gives

⟨F,𝒦​G⟩ν=(𝒥∗​F)⊤​(𝒥∗​G)=⟨𝒦​F,G⟩ν,⟨F,𝒦​F⟩ν=‖𝒥∗​F‖2≥0.\langle F,\mathcal{K}G\rangle_{\nu}=(\mathcal{J}^{*}F)^{\top}(\mathcal{J}^{*}G)=\langle\mathcal{K}F,G\rangle_{\nu},\qquad\langle F,\mathcal{K}F\rangle_{\nu}=\|\mathcal{J}^{*}F\|^{2}\geq 0.

By the chain rule, the logit velocity generated by uu is 𝒥​u=𝒦​B\mathcal{J}u=\mathcal{K}B. Thus ⟨B,z˙⟩ν=‖u‖2\langle B,\dot{z}\rangle_{\nu}=\|u\|^{2}. Since P>0P>0, the strictly convex quadratic α↦‖z˙−α​B‖ν2\alpha\mapsto\|\dot{z}-\alpha B\|_{\nu}^{2} has its unique minimum at α=⟨B,z˙⟩ν/P\alpha=\langle B,\dot{z}\rangle_{\nu}/P. This is Ξ\Xi, and the residual has the stated orthogonality.

For Dg>0D_{g}>0, multiplication of the defined ratios gives Ξ=A​C\Xi=AC and ‖u‖2=P​A​C\|u\|^{2}=PAC. Expanding a centered squared norm gives

𝔼ν​‖g−u‖2=𝔼ν​‖g‖2−2​u⊤​𝔼ν​g+‖u‖2=Dg−‖u‖2≥0.\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\|g-u\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\|g\|^{2}-2u^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{\nu}g+\|u\|^{2}=D_{g}-\|u\|^{2}\geq 0.

This proves C≤1C\leq 1 and its equality condition; nonnegativity of CC and its zero condition follow from its numerator. If Dg=0D_{g}=0, every nonnegative summand ν⁡(s)​‖g⁡(s)‖2\nu(s)\|g(s)\|^{2} vanishes, so g=u=0g=u=0. If P=0P=0, the same argument first gives B=0B=0, then g=u=0g=u=0. These cases cannot be handled by cancelling zero denominators. ∎

Proposition C.7 (Joint singular modes).

Stack the blocks ν⁡(s)​Φ​(s)\sqrt{\nu(s)}\Phi(s) into 𝖩∈ℝNν×d\mathsf{J}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\nu}\times d} and ν⁡(s)​B​(s)\sqrt{\nu(s)}B(s) into 𝐁∈ℝNν\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\nu}}. Let the compact singular-value decomposition be 𝖩=U​Σ​V⊤\mathsf{J}=U\Sigma V^{\top}, of rank rr, with orthonormal columns Uj,VjU_{j},V_{j} and positive singular values σj\sigma_{j}. If P>0P>0,

u=∑j=1rσj​(Uj⊤​𝐁)​Vj,Ξ=∑j=1rσj2​|Uj⊤​𝐁|2‖𝐁‖2.u=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_{j}(U_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{B})V_{j},\qquad\Xi=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_{j}^{2}\frac{|U_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{B}|^{2}}{\|\mathbf{B}\|^{2}}. (12)

The component of 𝐁\mathbf{B} orthogonal to range⁡(𝖩)\operatorname{range}(\mathsf{J}) produces zero parameter response.

Proof.

The stacking gives 𝖩⊤​𝐁=∑sν⁡(s)​Φ​(s)⊤​B​(s)=u\mathsf{J}^{\top}\mathbf{B}=\sum_{s}\nu(s)\Phi(s)^{\top}B(s)=u and ‖𝐁‖2=P\|\mathbf{B}\|^{2}=P. Substitution of the singular-value decomposition proves the first identity. Since Vi⊤Vj=𝟏{i=j}V_{i}^{\top}V_{j}=\mathbf{1}\{i=j\}, its squared norm is ∑jσj2​|Uj⊤​𝐁|2\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}^{2}|U_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{B}|^{2}; division by PP proves the second. Finally 𝖩⊤​𝐁⟂=V​Σ​U⊤​𝐁⟂=0\mathsf{J}^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{\perp}=V\Sigma U^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{\perp}=0 when U⊤​𝐁⟂=0U^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{\perp}=0. If r=0r=0, these are empty sums and u=Ξ=0u=\Xi=0. ∎

Joint modes span multiple prefixes and tokens. Their parameter-space components are orthogonal, whereas individual per-prefix gradients need not be. Strong cancellation between local gradients is therefore compatible with large self-kernel responses but a small joint response; independently sorted self-kernel spectra do not determine Equation 12.

Proposition C.8 (Coherence and interference).

For independent s,s′∼νs,s^{\prime}\sim\nu,

‖u‖2=𝔼⁡⟨g⁡(s),g⁡(s′)⟩=𝔼ν​‖g⁡(s)‖2−12​𝔼​‖g⁡(s)−g⁡(s′)‖2.\|u\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}\langle g(s),g(s^{\prime})\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\|g(s)\|^{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|g(s)-g(s^{\prime})\|^{2}.

If B=∑m=1MB(m)B=\sum_{m=1}^{M}B^{(m)} is any finite field decomposition and u(m)=𝔼ν​[Φ⊤​B(m)]u^{(m)}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[\Phi^{\top}B^{(m)}], then ‖u‖2=∑m‖u(m)‖2+2​∑m<n⟨u(m),u(n)⟩\|u\|^{2}=\sum_{m}\|u^{(m)}\|^{2}+2\sum_{m<n}\langle u^{(m)},u^{(n)}\rangle.

Proof.

Independence gives the explicit finite-sum identity

𝔼⁡⟨g⁡(s),g⁡(s′)⟩=∑s,s′ν⁡(s)​ν​(s′)​g​(s)⊤​g​(s′)=(∑sν⁡(s)​g​(s))⊤​(∑s′ν⁡(s′)​g​(s′)).\mathbb{E}\langle g(s),g(s^{\prime})\rangle=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}}\nu(s)\nu(s^{\prime})g(s)^{\top}g(s^{\prime})=\left(\sum_{s}\nu(s)g(s)\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{s^{\prime}}\nu(s^{\prime})g(s^{\prime})\right).

This is ‖u‖2\|u\|^{2}. Expanding the squared difference and using the identical marginals yields 𝔼​‖g⁡(s)−g⁡(s′)‖2=2​Dg−2​‖u‖2\mathbb{E}\|g(s)-g(s^{\prime})\|^{2}=2D_{g}-2\|u\|^{2}. The field decomposition gives u=∑mu(m)u=\sum_{m}u^{(m)} by linearity, and the last formula follows by expanding the square and collecting both copies of each off-diagonal inner product. ∎

Proposition C.9 (Finite-sample correction of the mean-gradient energy).

Let g1,…,gng_{1},\ldots,g_{n}, n>1n>1, be independent identically distributed parameter vectors with finite second moment and mean uu. Define g¯=n−1​∑igi\bar{g}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}g_{i} and D^g=n−1​∑i‖gi‖2\widehat{D}_{g}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\|g_{i}\|^{2}. Then

U^=n​‖g¯‖2−D^gn−1=1n⁡(n−1)​∑i≠jgi⊤​gj\widehat{U}=\frac{n\|\bar{g}\|^{2}-\widehat{D}_{g}}{n-1}=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}g_{i}^{\top}g_{j}

has expectation ‖u‖2\|u\|^{2}.

Proof.

Expanding n2​‖g¯‖2n^{2}\|\bar{g}\|^{2} gives ∑i‖gi‖2+∑i≠jgi⊤​gj\sum_{i}\|g_{i}\|^{2}+\sum_{i\neq j}g_{i}^{\top}g_{j}. Subtracting n​D^g=∑i‖gi‖2n\widehat{D}_{g}=\sum_{i}\|g_{i}\|^{2} and dividing by n⁡(n−1)n(n-1) proves the second expression. Independence gives 𝔼⁡[gi⊤​gj]=(𝔼​gi)⊤​(𝔼​gj)=‖u‖2\mathbb{E}[g_{i}^{\top}g_{j}]=(\mathbb{E}g_{i})^{\top}(\mathbb{E}g_{j})=\|u\|^{2} for each of its n⁡(n−1)n(n-1) terms. Thus its expectation is ‖u‖2\|u\|^{2}. The finite second moment makes every term integrable. Positive clipping and division by the random D^g\widehat{D}_{g} are nonlinear, so the bias of the resulting coherence ratio falls outside this linear expectation calculation. Other sampling designs, including sampling without replacement from a fixed finite population, require their own design-specific bias calculation. ∎

Policy-level observation of a logit response.

For a fixed vector w⁡(x)w(x) with 𝟏⊤​w​(x)=0\mathbf{1}^{\top}w(x)=0,

w(x)⊤[zθ′(x)−zθ(x)]=w(x)⊤[logpθ′(⋅∣x)−logpθ(⋅∣x)].w(x)^{\top}[z_{\theta^{\prime}}(x)-z_{\theta}(x)]=w(x)^{\top}[\log p_{\theta^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid x)-\log p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)].

Indeed, logpθ=zθ−log∑aezθ​(a)𝟏\log p_{\theta}=z_{\theta}-\log\sum_{a}e^{z_{\theta}(a)}\mathbf{1}, and both scalar-normalizer terms disappear under w⊤w^{\top}. The identity holds for finite displacements, for zero-extended contrasts on a recorded support, and for centered and uncentered training fields alike. The experimental contrast is specified in Section D.3.

C.4 Why the frozen spectral probe measures accessibility

Connection to Section 3.2 and the fixed-bank diagnostic in Section 3.4. All time dependence below is in the tangent map; the bank, coordinates, and numerical field are fixed.

Proposition C.10 (Frozen-field Rayleigh expansion).

Let P0=𝔼ν0​‖B0‖2>0P_{0}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{0}}\|B_{0}\|^{2}>0, and define on nonzero-request sites

A⁡[B]=𝔼ν​[B​(s)⊤​K​(s,s)​B​(s)]𝔼ν​‖B⁡(s)‖2.A[B]=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[B(s)^{\top}K(s,s)B(s)]}{\mathbb{E}_{\nu}\|B(s)\|^{2}}. (13)

Let (λj,t​(s),vj,t​(s))(\lambda_{j,t}(s),v_{j,t}(s)) be a complete orthonormal eigendecomposition of Kt​(s,s)K_{t}(s,s). Then

at​(s)\displaystyle a_{t}(s) =b0​(s)⊤​Kt​(s,s)​b0​(s)=∑jλj,t​(s)​|vj,t​(s)⊤​b0​(s)|2,\displaystyle=b_{0}(s)^{\top}K_{t}(s,s)b_{0}(s)=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j,t}(s)|v_{j,t}(s)^{\top}b_{0}(s)|^{2}, (14)

The weights sum to one. In particular, At​[B0]A_{t}[B_{0}] is constant whenever the self-kernels are constant on the bank.

Proof.

For each site, ‖Φ​(s)⊤​B​(s)‖2=B​(s)⊤​Φ​(s)​Φ​(s)⊤​B​(s)=B​(s)⊤​K​(s,s)​B​(s)\|\Phi(s)^{\top}B(s)\|^{2}=B(s)^{\top}\Phi(s)\Phi(s)^{\top}B(s)=B(s)^{\top}K(s,s)B(s). The live quantity At​[Bt]A_{t}[B_{t}] can also change through its field and energy weights. The frozen collective gain is Ξt​[B0]=At​[B0]​Ct​[B0]\Xi_{t}[B_{0}]=A_{t}[B_{0}]C_{t}[B_{0}] when the denominators are nonzero; both factors use B0B_{0}, whereas At​[B0]​Ct​[Bt]A_{t}[B_{0}]C_{t}[B_{t}] mixes two fields and is a different quantity.

C.5 Routing and conditional drift on moving prefix populations

Connection to Section 3.3, Equations 5 and 6. Let mobs​(x)≥0m^{\rm obs}(x)\geq 0 be a fixed weight on the nonterminal prefixes of the observation tree. Assume at least one eligible prefix has positive reach probability, and define

νt​(x)=mobs​(x)​dt​(x)Ztobs,Ztobs=∑xmobs​(x)​dt​(x)>0.\nu_{t}(x)=\frac{m^{\rm obs}(x)d_{t}(x)}{Z_{t}^{\rm obs}},\qquad Z_{t}^{\rm obs}=\sum_{x}m^{\rm obs}(x)d_{t}(x)>0. (15)

This is normalization of expected weighted counts, which allows fixed depth masks, context classes defined by a fixed reference learner, and empirical minibatches of unequal length.

Proposition C.11 (Routing and conditional drift).

Let Yt​(x)Y_{t}(x) be a scalar readout that is continuous and piecewise C1C^{1} along the parameter path, and put JY​(t)=∑xνt​(x)​Yt​(x)J_{Y}(t)=\sum_{x}\nu_{t}(x)Y_{t}(x). For a positive-reach prefix with ancestry (xj,aj)j<h⁡(x)(x_{j},a_{j})_{j<h(x)}, define

Then, almost everywhere,

ν˙t​(x)\displaystyle\dot{\nu}_{t}(x) =νt​(x)​(λt​(x)−𝔼νt​λt),\displaystyle=\nu_{t}(x)\bigl(\lambda_{t}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}\lambda_{t}\bigr),
J˙Y​(t)\displaystyle\dot{J}_{Y}(t) =RY​(t)+DY​(t),RY​(t)=Covνt⁡(Yt,λt),DY​(t)=𝔼νt​Y˙t.\displaystyle=R_{Y}(t)+D_{Y}(t),\qquad R_{Y}(t)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{t}}(Y_{t},\lambda_{t}),\quad D_{Y}(t)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}\dot{Y}_{t}.

If Yt​(x)=Y⁡(zt​(x),x)Y_{t}(x)=Y(z_{t}(x),x) for a C1C^{1} local function YY with no explicit time dependence, then Y˙t​(x)=∇zY​(zt​(x),x)⊤​vt​(x)\dot{Y}_{t}(x)=\nabla_{z}Y(z_{t}(x),x)^{\top}v_{t}(x). Under raw flow, vt=Kt​Γtv_{t}=K_{t}\Gamma_{t}. For every subinterval [a,b][a,b], JY​(b)−JY​(a)=∫ab(RY+DY)​𝑑tJ_{Y}(b)-J_{Y}(a)=\int_{a}^{b}(R_{Y}+D_{Y})\,dt.

Proof.

For fixed xx, the prompt bxb_{x} and all tokens in its ancestry are fixed while training time changes. Thus

dt​(x)=β⁡(bx)​∏j<h⁡(x)πt​(aj∣xj),∂tlog⁡dt​(x)=∑j<h⁡(x)∂tlog⁡πt​(aj∣xj).d_{t}(x)=\beta(b_{x})\prod_{j<h(x)}\pi_{t}(a_{j}\mid x_{j}),\qquad\partial_{t}\log d_{t}(x)=\sum_{j<h(x)}\partial_{t}\log\pi_{t}(a_{j}\mid x_{j}).

This proves the formula for λt\lambda_{t}; at a root the product is empty and λt=0\lambda_{t}=0. Also d˙t​(x)=dt​(x)​λt​(x)\dot{d}_{t}(x)=d_{t}(x)\lambda_{t}(x). Differentiating the finite normalizer gives

Z˙tobsZtobs=∑xmobs​(x)​dt​(x)​λt​(x)Ztobs=𝔼νt​λt.\frac{\dot{Z}_{t}^{\rm obs}}{Z_{t}^{\rm obs}}=\frac{\sum_{x}m^{\rm obs}(x)d_{t}(x)\lambda_{t}(x)}{Z_{t}^{\rm obs}}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}\lambda_{t}.

The quotient rule now gives the asserted formula for ν˙t\dot{\nu}_{t} at each eligible site. For a site with zero fixed mask, both νt\nu_{t} and ν˙t\dot{\nu}_{t} are zero, so the same expression holds with that site omitted.

The product rule and the definition of covariance yield

J˙Y\displaystyle\dot{J}_{Y} =∑xν˙t​(x)​Yt​(x)+∑xνt​(x)​Y˙t​(x)\displaystyle=\sum_{x}\dot{\nu}_{t}(x)Y_{t}(x)+\sum_{x}\nu_{t}(x)\dot{Y}_{t}(x)
=𝔼νt​(Yt​λt)−(𝔼νt​Yt)​(𝔼νt​λt)+𝔼νt​Y˙t.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}(Y_{t}\lambda_{t})-(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}Y_{t})(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}\lambda_{t})+\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}\dot{Y}_{t}.

For a local readout, the chain rule gives Y˙t=∇zY⊤​z˙t\dot{Y}_{t}=\nabla_{z}Y^{\top}\dot{z}_{t}; the raw specialization follows from Section C.2. All functions are continuous and piecewise C1C^{1} on a finite partition of the compact interval. Integrating the derivative on each piece and telescoping the boundary values proves the final equality. ∎

The two roles of the same parameter change.

Define ℱ⁡(θg,θe)=∑xνθg​(x)​Yθe​(x)\mathcal{F}(\theta_{g},\theta_{e})=\sum_{x}\nu_{\theta_{g}}(x)Y_{\theta_{e}}(x). Applying the multivariable chain rule to ℱ⁡(θt,θt)\mathcal{F}(\theta_{t},\theta_{t}) gives its generator derivative ∑xν˙t​Yt=RY\sum_{x}\dot{\nu}_{t}Y_{t}=R_{Y} and evaluator derivative ∑xνt​Y˙t=DY\sum_{x}\nu_{t}\dot{Y}_{t}=D_{Y}. Both are contributions of the same parameter change to one derivative. A readout depending on the full parameter vector, rather than only the logits at xx, uses Y˙t​(x)=∇θYθ​(x)⊤​θ˙t\dot{Y}_{t}(x)=\nabla_{\theta}Y_{\theta}(x)^{\top}\dot{\theta}_{t} instead. This distinction will matter for continuation values.

If prompt weights or observation masks vary explicitly, the formula for λt\lambda_{t} alone is insufficient. On positive coordinates the quotient-rule calculation instead centers ∂tlog⁡[mtobs​(x)​dt​(x)]\partial_{t}\log[m_{t}^{\rm obs}(x)d_{t}(x)]; ∂tlog⁡dt\partial_{t}\log d_{t} includes ∂tlog⁡βt​(bx)\partial_{t}\log\beta_{t}(b_{x}) for a changing prompt law. Zero weights or changes of support require separate boundary accounting. The fixed-weight assumptions are therefore substantive.

C.6 Finite-window exposure and regenerated source weights

Connection to Section 3.3, Equation 7. Use a superscript tr{\rm tr} when training and observation employ different fixed prompt laws or samplers. In particular, τtr\tau_{\rm tr} can differ from the observation temperature. For a fixed training mask mtr​(s)≥0m^{\rm tr}(s)\geq 0, let

μt​(s)=mtr​(s)​dttr​(s)Zttr,Zttr=∑smtr​(s)​dttr​(s)>0.\mu_{t}(s)=\frac{m^{\rm tr}(s)d_{t}^{\rm tr}(s)}{Z_{t}^{\rm tr}},\qquad Z_{t}^{\rm tr}=\sum_{s}m^{\rm tr}(s)d_{t}^{\rm tr}(s)>0.

The following proposition assumes one fixed eligible support throughout the interval, as guaranteed by Assumption C.1. Merely sharing some positive-support states at the endpoints is not sufficient for the unrestricted normalization formula.

Proposition C.12 (Source reweighting across a training window).

For a≤ba\leq b, let Λa:b(s)=∫abλttr(s)dt\Lambda_{a:b}(s)=\int_{a}^{b}\lambda_{t}^{\rm tr}(s)\,dt, where λttr\lambda_{t}^{\rm tr} is the ancestral log reach-probability velocity under the training sampler. On every allowed prefix,

dbtr​(s)datr​(s)=eΛa:b(s),Λa:c(s)=Λa:b(s)+Λb:c(s)(a≤b≤c).\frac{d_{b}^{\rm tr}(s)}{d_{a}^{\rm tr}(s)}=e^{\Lambda_{a:b}(s)},\qquad\Lambda_{a:c}(s)=\Lambda_{a:b}(s)+\Lambda_{b:c}(s)\quad(a\leq b\leq c). (16)

For each eligible source prefix,

μb(s)=μa(s)eΛa:b(s)𝔼v∼μaeΛa:b(v),Γb(s)=μb(s)Bb(s).\mu_{b}(s)=\frac{\mu_{a}(s)e^{\Lambda_{a:b}(s)}}{\mathbb{E}_{v\sim\mu_{a}}e^{\Lambda_{a:b}(v)}},\qquad\Gamma_{b}(s)=\mu_{b}(s)B_{b}(s). (17)

A zero fixed mask stays zero.

Proof.

By Proposition C.11 with the training sampler, ∂tlog⁡dttr​(s)=λttr​(s)\partial_{t}\log d_{t}^{\rm tr}(s)=\lambda_{t}^{\rm tr}(s) on each smooth piece. Integrating and telescoping gives logdbtr(s)−logdatr(s)=Λa:b(s)\log d_{b}^{\rm tr}(s)-\log d_{a}^{\rm tr}(s)=\Lambda_{a:b}(s). Exponentiating proves the ratio, and additivity of the integral proves the second identity.

Because the eligible set is the same at both endpoints, substitution into the entire source normalizer is valid:

Zbtr\displaystyle Z_{b}^{\rm tr} =∑smtr(s)datr(s)eΛa:b(s)\displaystyle=\sum_{s}m^{\rm tr}(s)d_{a}^{\rm tr}(s)e^{\Lambda_{a:b}(s)}
=Zatr∑sμa(s)eΛa:b(s).\displaystyle=Z_{a}^{\rm tr}\sum_{s}\mu_{a}(s)e^{\Lambda_{a:b}(s)}.

The expectation is strictly positive and finite, since it is a finite sum of positive terms on the nonempty eligible set. Dividing mtr​(s)​dbtr​(s)m^{\rm tr}(s)d_{b}^{\rm tr}(s) by this expression for ZbtrZ_{b}^{\rm tr} proves Equation 17. The expression for Γb\Gamma_{b} defines the regenerated request population with the current numerical field BbB_{b}. If mtr​(s)=0m^{\rm tr}(s)=0, both endpoint weights are zero directly from their definition. ∎

An eligible prefix can be absent from a finite recorded batch while having positive population weight at every checkpoint. The reference in Equation 17 is the population μa\mu_{a}, which includes such prefixes. At a root, Λ=0\Lambda=0, although normalization by the total expected token count can change its source weight.

C.6.1 Finite-batch extraction and native checkpoints

Proposition C.13 (Transport of a normalized batch extraction).

Let 𝔅\mathfrak{B} be a finite batch space and Patr,PbtrP_{a}^{\rm tr},P_{b}^{\rm tr} two batch laws with identical positive support. For each batch ℬ\mathcal{B}, let μ^ℬ​(s)≥0\widehat{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}}(s)\geq 0 be an extraction rule with ∑sμ^ℬ​(s)=1\sum_{s}\widehat{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}}(s)=1, determined only by the batch text. Set μt​(s)=𝔼Pttr​μ^ℬ​(s)\mu_{t}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{P_{t}^{\rm tr}}\widehat{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}}(s) and Λa:b(ℬ)=log[Pbtr(ℬ)/Patr(ℬ)]\Lambda_{a:b}(\mathcal{B})=\log[P_{b}^{\rm tr}(\mathcal{B})/P_{a}^{\rm tr}(\mathcal{B})]. Then

μb(s)=𝔼Patr[μ^ℬ(s)eΛa:b(ℬ)],𝔼PatreΛa:b(ℬ)=1.\mu_{b}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{P_{a}^{\rm tr}}\!\bigl[\widehat{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}}(s)e^{\Lambda_{a:b}(\mathcal{B})}\bigr],\qquad\mathbb{E}_{P_{a}^{\rm tr}}e^{\Lambda_{a:b}(\mathcal{B})}=1. (18)
Proof.

Expand the first expectation and cancel its positive probability factor:

∑ℬPatr​(ℬ)​μ^ℬ​(s)​Pbtr​(ℬ)Patr​(ℬ)=∑ℬPbtr​(ℬ)​μ^ℬ​(s)=μb​(s).\sum_{\mathcal{B}}P_{a}^{\rm tr}(\mathcal{B})\widehat{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}}(s)\frac{P_{b}^{\rm tr}(\mathcal{B})}{P_{a}^{\rm tr}(\mathcal{B})}=\sum_{\mathcal{B}}P_{b}^{\rm tr}(\mathcal{B})\widehat{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}}(s)=\mu_{b}(s).

Taking μ^ℬ​(s)\widehat{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}}(s) out of this calculation and replacing it by one gives ∑ℬPbtr​(ℬ)=1\sum_{\mathcal{B}}P_{b}^{\rm tr}(\mathcal{B})=1. If the batch responses are independent, its probability is their product, so its log likelihood ratio is the sum of their complete-trajectory log ratios. Conditional independence given a fixed shared prompt schedule gives the same factorization conditional on that schedule. ∎

For example, if Ns​(ℬ)N_{s}(\mathcal{B}) is the eligible count at ss, batch normalization gives μ^ℬ​(s)=Ns​(ℬ)/∑vNv​(ℬ)\widehat{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}}(s)=N_{s}(\mathcal{B})/\sum_{v}N_{v}(\mathcal{B}) when the denominator is positive. Its expectation is generally not 𝔼Ns/𝔼∑vNv\mathbb{E}N_{s}/\mathbb{E}\sum_{v}N_{v}. Thus the random normalization must stay inside Equation 18; no additional ratio of expectations is introduced. A rule for batches with no eligible positions must be specified before defining a normalized extraction. If extraction also depends on the learner after fixing the text, transport uses the endpoint rule μ^b,ℬ\widehat{\mu}_{b,\mathcal{B}}, not an unchanged rule from time aa.

Native checkpoint identity.

For discrete checkpoints k1<k2k_{1}<k_{2}, assume that every token in the chosen prefix has positive sampler probability at every intermediate checkpoint. Then

Λk1:k2(s)\displaystyle\Lambda_{k_{1}:k_{2}}(s) :=∑k=k1k2−1∑j<h⁡(s)log⁡πk+1tr​(aj∣sj)πktr​(aj∣sj)\displaystyle:=\sum_{k=k_{1}}^{k_{2}-1}\sum_{j<h(s)}\log\frac{\pi_{k+1}^{\rm tr}(a_{j}\mid s_{j})}{\pi_{k}^{\rm tr}(a_{j}\mid s_{j})}
=∑j<h⁡(s)log⁡πk2tr​(aj∣sj)πk1tr​(aj∣sj)=log⁡dk2tr​(s)dk1tr​(s).\displaystyle=\sum_{j<h(s)}\log\frac{\pi_{k_{2}}^{\rm tr}(a_{j}\mid s_{j})}{\pi_{k_{1}}^{\rm tr}(a_{j}\mid s_{j})}=\log\frac{d_{k_{2}}^{\rm tr}(s)}{d_{k_{1}}^{\rm tr}(s)}.

The first equality telescopes the finite sum over checkpoints for each token; the second multiplies the ancestral probability factors and cancels the fixed prompt law. The normalizer calculation in Proposition C.12 then applies unchanged on a fixed eligible support. The identity holds for any optimizer and any learning rate. If a token has zero probability at an intermediate checkpoint, the per-step logarithms above need not exist even when both endpoint probabilities are positive; the endpoint ratio can still be used directly where it is defined.

C.6.2 Changing support and nonsmooth readouts

Proposition C.14 (Explicit support accounting).

Let Pa,PbP_{a},P_{b} be probability laws on a common finite universe, let 𝒞=supp⁡Pa∩supp⁡Pb\mathcal{C}=\operatorname{supp}P_{a}\cap\operatorname{supp}P_{b}, and let FF be a bounded real function. Define eΛ⁡(v)=Pb​(v)/Pa​(v)e^{\Lambda(v)}=P_{b}(v)/P_{a}(v) only for v∈𝒞v\in\mathcal{C}. Then

𝔼Pb​F−𝔼Pa​F\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{P_{b}}F-\mathbb{E}_{P_{a}}F =∑v∈𝒞Pa​(v)​F​(v)​(eΛ⁡(v)−1)\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{C}}P_{a}(v)F(v)(e^{\Lambda(v)}-1)
+∑v∈supp⁡Pb∖𝒞Pb(v)F(v)−∑v∈supp⁡Pa∖𝒞Pa(v)F(v).\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{v\in\operatorname{supp}P_{b}\setminus\mathcal{C}}P_{b}(v)F(v)-\sum_{v\in\operatorname{supp}P_{a}\setminus\mathcal{C}}P_{a}(v)F(v).

The absolute value of the last two terms together is at most ‖F‖∞​[Pb​(𝒞c)+Pa​(𝒞c)]\|F\|_{\infty}[P_{b}(\mathcal{C}^{c})+P_{a}(\mathcal{C}^{c})].

Proof.

Split each expectation into its contribution on 𝒞\mathcal{C} and on its complement. On 𝒞\mathcal{C}, replace Pb​(v)P_{b}(v) by Pa​(v)​eΛ⁡(v)P_{a}(v)e^{\Lambda(v)} and subtract. This gives the identity. Applying the triangle inequality and |F⁡(v)|≤‖F‖∞|F(v)|\leq\|F\|_{\infty} to the remaining sums gives the bound. ∎

In particular, ∑v∈𝒞Pa​(v)​eΛ⁡(v)=Pb​(𝒞)\sum_{v\in\mathcal{C}}P_{a}(v)e^{\Lambda(v)}=P_{b}(\mathcal{C}), which need not be one. Common-support ratios do not recover newly created mass or, by themselves, the full normalization of a changed source. The proposition applies to complete-trajectory laws, batch laws, or normalized source laws. Changed prompt sets and masks require the same care.

The local top-16 loss in Section E.1 can change its expression when the selected support changes. If a readout path has finitely many such changes and is piecewise C1C^{1} with one-sided limits, integration over each smooth piece gives

J⁡(b)−J⁡(a)=∫abJ˙​(t)​𝑑t+∑ti∈(a,b)[J⁡(ti+)−J⁡(ti−)],J(b)-J(a)=\int_{a}^{b}\dot{J}(t)\,dt+\sum_{t_{i}\in(a,b)}[J(t_{i}^{+})-J(t_{i}^{-})],

with endpoints taken on their respective one-sided branches. The formula follows by telescoping the integrals and inserting the jumps; a continuous branch switch has zero jump. Smooth-flow integrals are asserted only under this regularity; the finite four-cell identity below remains valid whenever its four scores are finite. For an exogenously fixed source, the response and outcome laws still hold, while the source’s own generating rule replaces the on-policy source-tilt formula.

C.7 Exact symmetric endpoint accounting and its path limit

Connection to Section 3.3, Equation 8. The four-cell estimator is exactly additive at finite endpoints; the difference between its individual components and the continuous routing and drift integrals is computed and bounded in Proposition C.17.

Proposition C.15 (Symmetric endpoint accounting).

Let νa,νb\nu_{a},\nu_{b} be any two probability vectors on the union of two finite rollout banks, and let Ya,YbY_{a},Y_{b} be finite readouts defined on that union. With Mi​j=∑xνi​(x)​Yj​(x)M_{ij}=\sum_{x}\nu_{i}(x)Y_{j}(x), define

R^a:b=12[(Mb​a−Ma​a)+(Mb​b−Ma​b)],D^a:b=12[(Ma​b−Ma​a)+(Mb​b−Mb​a)].\widehat{R}_{a:b}=\tfrac{1}{2}[(M_{ba}-M_{aa})+(M_{bb}-M_{ab})],\qquad\widehat{D}_{a:b}=\tfrac{1}{2}[(M_{ab}-M_{aa})+(M_{bb}-M_{ba})]. (19)

Using ⟨ν,Y⟩:=∑xν⁡(x)​Y​(x)\langle\nu,Y\rangle:=\sum_{x}\nu(x)Y(x) for the distribution–readout pairing,

R^a:b=⟨νb−νa,Ya+Yb2⟩,D^a:b=⟨νa+νb2,Yb−Ya⟩,\widehat{R}_{a:b}=\left\langle\nu_{b}-\nu_{a},\frac{Y_{a}+Y_{b}}{2}\right\rangle,\qquad\widehat{D}_{a:b}=\left\langle\frac{\nu_{a}+\nu_{b}}{2},Y_{b}-Y_{a}\right\rangle,

and R^a:b+D^a:b=Mb​b−Ma​a\widehat{R}_{a:b}+\widehat{D}_{a:b}=M_{bb}-M_{aa}.

Remark C.16.

The inner products can be intuitively interpreted: for routing R^a:b\widehat{R}_{a:b}, we measure the effect of changing the rollout distribution vtv_{t} while holding the readout to the averaged Ya+Yb2\frac{Y_{a}+Y_{b}}{2}; the drift estimator holds the rollout distribution averaged while varying the readouts (how much fitting happened over the period (a,b)(a,b)).

Proof.

Set Δ​ν=νb−νa\Delta\nu=\nu_{b}-\nu_{a} and Δ​Y=Yb−Ya\Delta Y=Y_{b}-Y_{a}. Bilinearity gives

Mb​b−Ma​a=⟨Δ​ν,Ya⟩+⟨νa,Δ​Y⟩+⟨Δ​ν,Δ​Y⟩.M_{bb}-M_{aa}=\langle\Delta\nu,Y_{a}\rangle+\langle\nu_{a},\Delta Y\rangle+\langle\Delta\nu,\Delta Y\rangle.

Expanding the four terms in Equation 19 yields

R^a:b=⟨Δν,Ya⟩+12⟨Δν,ΔY⟩,D^a:b=⟨νa,ΔY⟩+12⟨Δν,ΔY⟩.\widehat{R}_{a:b}=\langle\Delta\nu,Y_{a}\rangle+\tfrac{1}{2}\langle\Delta\nu,\Delta Y\rangle,\qquad\widehat{D}_{a:b}=\langle\nu_{a},\Delta Y\rangle+\tfrac{1}{2}\langle\Delta\nu,\Delta Y\rangle.

∎

Proposition C.17 (Difference from the path-integrated channels).

Suppose νt,Yt\nu_{t},Y_{t} are C1C^{1} on time interval [a,b][a,b], and write Ra:b=∫ab⟨ν˙t,Yt⟩dtR_{a:b}=\int_{a}^{b}\langle\dot{\nu}_{t},Y_{t}\rangle\,dt and Da:b=∫ab⟨νt,Y˙t⟩dtD_{a:b}=\int_{a}^{b}\langle\nu_{t},\dot{Y}_{t}\rangle\,dt. Then

|R^a:b−Ra:b|=|D^a:b−Da:b|≤(b−a)312(LνMY+MνLY).|\widehat{R}_{a:b}-R_{a:b}|=|\widehat{D}_{a:b}-D_{a:b}|\leq\frac{(b-a)^{3}}{12}(L_{\nu}M_{Y}+M_{\nu}L_{Y}).

Substitute νb−νa=∫abν˙t​𝑑t\nu_{b}-\nu_{a}=\int_{a}^{b}\dot{\nu}_{t}\,dt in the pairing for R^\widehat{R} and subtract Ra:bR_{a:b}. Since the sums of the two channels both equal JY​(b)−JY​(a)J_{Y}(b)-J_{Y}(a), their errors have opposite signs. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives

‖Ya+Yb2−Yt‖∞≤12​LY​[(t−a)+(b−t)]=12​LY​(b−a).\left\|\frac{Y_{a}+Y_{b}}{2}-Y_{t}\right\|_{\infty}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}L_{Y}[(t-a)+(b-t)]=\tfrac{1}{2}L_{Y}(b-a).

Applying |⟨v,y⟩|≤‖v‖1​‖y‖∞|\langle v,y\rangle|\leq\|v\|_{1}\|y\|_{\infty} and integrating proves the C1C^{1} bound.

For the sharper result, insert 12​(Ya+Yb)−Yt=12​(∫tbY˙r​𝑑r−∫atY˙r​𝑑r)\frac{1}{2}(Y_{a}+Y_{b})-Y_{t}=\frac{1}{2}(\int_{t}^{b}\dot{Y}_{r}\,dr-\int_{a}^{t}\dot{Y}_{r}\,dr) into the exact error. Reordering these finite-dimensional integrals gives

R^−R=12​∫a≤r<t≤b[⟨ν˙r,Y˙t⟩−⟨ν˙t,Y˙r⟩]​𝑑r​𝑑t.\widehat{R}-R=\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{a\leq r<t\leq b}\bigl[\langle\dot{\nu}_{r},\dot{Y}_{t}\rangle-\langle\dot{\nu}_{t},\dot{Y}_{r}\rangle\bigr]\,dr\,dt.

Add and subtract ⟨ν˙r,Y˙r⟩\langle\dot{\nu}_{r},\dot{Y}_{r}\rangle in the integrand. Its absolute value is bounded by Lν​‖Y˙t−Y˙r‖∞+‖ν˙t−ν˙r‖1​LY≤(Lν​MY+Mν​LY)​(t−r)L_{\nu}\|\dot{Y}_{t}-\dot{Y}_{r}\|_{\infty}+\|\dot{\nu}_{t}-\dot{\nu}_{r}\|_{1}L_{Y}\leq(L_{\nu}M_{Y}+M_{\nu}L_{Y})(t-r). For a partition of a fixed interval with largest width hh, the finite totals telescope exactly. Summing the C1C^{1} bound gives a channel error at most Lν​LY​(b−a)​h/2L_{\nu}L_{Y}(b-a)h/2, tending to zero as h→0h\to 0; the C2C^{2} bound gives order h2h^{2} instead.

Scope.

The path limit is a population statement; finite-sample differences between empirical banks, checkpoint substitutions, prompt-composition changes, and support-switch jumps lie outside it, and Sections E.1 and E.6 give the corresponding experimental controls. At a fixed finite partition the allocation is a symmetric endpoint convention.

C.8 Continuation values and completed outcomes

Connection to Section 3.3, Equation 9. Recall that a terminal score is a fixed function of a completed rollout. Now, fix a bounded, model-parameter-independent function Y:𝒯→ℝY:\mathcal{T}\to\mathbb{R}. Write JY​(t)=𝔼Πt​YJ_{Y}(t)=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi_{t}}Y for the expectation of the terminal score over the time-tt generative distribution. For a non-terminal prefix xx, define

VtY​(x)=𝔼t​[Y∣x​ is reached],QtY​(x,a)=VtY​(x⊕a),𝒜tY​(x,a)=QtY​(x,a)−VtY​(x).V_{t}^{Y}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{t}[Y\mid x\text{ is reached}],\qquad Q_{t}^{Y}(x,a)=V_{t}^{Y}(x\oplus a),\qquad\mathcal{A}_{t}^{Y}(x,a)=Q_{t}^{Y}(x,a)-V_{t}^{Y}(x).

For terminal xx, we simply adopt the convention of VtY​(x)=Y⁡(x)V_{t}^{Y}(x)=Y(x). These are finite conditional expectations under the student’s current sampler with its remaining generation budget. Positivity on the fixed allowed autoregressive tree makes them well-defined. Conditioning on the next action gives VtY​(x)=∑aπt​(a∣x)​QtY​(x,a)V_{t}^{Y}(x)=\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid x)Q_{t}^{Y}(x,a) and ∑aπt​(a∣x)​𝒜tY​(x,a)=0\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid x)\mathcal{A}_{t}^{Y}(x,a)=0.

Proposition C.18 (Recombining exposure and continuation change).

For an integer 0≤h≤Hmax0\leq h\leq H_{\max}, let 𝒞h\mathcal{C}_{h} contain every allowed node at depth hh and every terminal node of depth less than hh. Then ∑x∈𝒞hdt​(x)=1\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}d_{t}(x)=1, and

JY​(t)\displaystyle J_{Y}(t) =∑x∈𝒞hdt​(x)​VtY​(x),\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}d_{t}(x)V_{t}^{Y}(x), (20)
J˙Y​(t)\displaystyle\dot{J}_{Y}(t) =∑x∈𝒞hd˙t​(x)​VtY​(x)+∑x∈𝒞hdt​(x)​V˙tY​(x).\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}\dot{d}_{t}(x)V_{t}^{Y}(x)+\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}d_{t}(x)\dot{V}_{t}^{Y}(x).

The first derivative term is the sum of the outcome contributions from decisions of depth less than hh; the second is the sum from decisions of depth at least hh. In particular, along any path satisfying the regularity conditions,

J˙Y(t)=∑x∈𝒮dt(x)𝔼a∼πt(⋅∣x)[ζt(x,a)𝒜tY(x,a)].\dot{J}_{Y}(t)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}}d_{t}(x)\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid x)}[\zeta_{t}(x,a)\mathcal{A}_{t}^{Y}(x,a)]. (21)

Under raw flow this equals

1τ​∑x∈𝒮∑sdt​(x)​[πt⊙𝒜tY]​(x)⊤​Kt​(x,s)​Γt​(s).\frac{1}{\tau}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{s}d_{t}(x)[\pi_{t}\odot\mathcal{A}_{t}^{Y}](x)^{\top}K_{t}(x,s)\Gamma_{t}(s).

Integrating from t⋆t_{\star} to TT yields Equation 9 in Section 3.3. If training and evaluation samplers differ, dt,πt,τd_{t},\pi_{t},\tau in this expression are the evaluation quantities, while Γt\Gamma_{t} uses the training source and field.

Proof.

Finite conditional values and the cut. Every trajectory ends by depth HmaxH_{\max}. It either reaches depth hh or terminates earlier, and therefore meets exactly one element of 𝒞h\mathcal{C}_{h}. The corresponding reach events are disjoint and exhaustive. Their probabilities sum to one, and conditioning the terminal score on this partition gives the first equality in Equation 20. At a nonterminal node, VtY​(x)V_{t}^{Y}(x) is a finite sum of terminal labels multiplied by products of suffix transition probabilities; at a terminal node it is the fixed label. Thus these values are continuous and piecewise C1C^{1}. The product rule proves the second equality.

Differentiating a continuation. For each nonterminal xx, set

𝔥t​(x)=∑aπt​(a∣x)​ζt​(x,a)​𝒜tY​(x,a).\mathfrak{h}_{t}(x)=\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid x)\zeta_{t}(x,a)\mathcal{A}_{t}^{Y}(x,a).

Differentiate the finite recursion VtY​(x)=∑aπt​(a∣x)​VtY​(x⊕a)V_{t}^{Y}(x)=\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid x)V_{t}^{Y}(x\oplus a). By Lemma C.2, π˙t=πt​ζt\dot{\pi}_{t}=\pi_{t}\zeta_{t} and ∑aπt​ζt=0\sum_{a}\pi_{t}\zeta_{t}=0, so

V˙tY​(x)=𝔥t​(x)+∑aπt​(a∣x)​V˙tY​(x⊕a).\dot{V}_{t}^{Y}(x)=\mathfrak{h}_{t}(x)+\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid x)\dot{V}_{t}^{Y}(x\oplus a).

At a terminal child the last derivative is zero. For a descendant yy of xx, let dt​(y∣x)d_{t}(y\mid x) be the product of transition probabilities from xx to yy, with dt​(x∣x)=1d_{t}(x\mid x)=1. Induction on the remaining depth proves

V˙tY(x)=∑y∈𝒮:y⪰xdt(y∣x)𝔥t(y).\dot{V}_{t}^{Y}(x)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in\mathcal{S}\,:\,y\succeq x\end{subarray}}d_{t}(y\mid x)\mathfrak{h}_{t}(y).

Indeed, if all children are terminal, (*) is precisely (**). Otherwise insert (**) for each nonterminal child into (*). Its descendant subtrees are disjoint, and multiplying a child’s descendant reach probability by πt​(a∣x)\pi_{t}(a\mid x) gives dt​(y∣x)d_{t}(y\mid x). This proves the induction step and counts every remaining decision exactly once.

Decisions after the cut. For a nonterminal yy of depth at least hh, the ancestry has a unique cut ancestor x∈𝒞hx\in\mathcal{C}_{h}. Also dt​(x)​dt​(y∣x)=dt​(y)d_{t}(x)d_{t}(y\mid x)=d_{t}(y). Multiplying (**) by dt​(x)d_{t}(x) and summing over the cut therefore gives

∑x∈𝒞hdt(x)V˙tY(x)=∑y∈𝒮:h⁡(y)≥hdt(y)𝔥t(y).\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}d_{t}(x)\dot{V}_{t}^{Y}(x)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in\mathcal{S}\,:\,h(y)\geq h\end{subarray}}d_{t}(y)\mathfrak{h}_{t}(y).

Terminal cut nodes have no descendants with decisions and contribute zero.

Decisions before the cut. The reach derivative at a cut node is d˙t​(c)=dt​(c)​∑j<h⁡(c)ζt​(cj,aj)\dot{d}_{t}(c)=d_{t}(c)\sum_{j<h(c)}\zeta_{t}(c_{j},a_{j}). ∑c∈𝒞h:c⪰x⊕adt(c)VtY(c)=dt(x)πt(a∣x)QtY(x,a).\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\in\mathcal{C}_{h}\,:\,c\succeq x\oplus a\end{subarray}}d_{t}(c)V_{t}^{Y}(c)=d_{t}(x)\pi_{t}(a\mid x)Q_{t}^{Y}(x,a).

To verify this equality, condition on reaching xx and selecting aa. The subsequent cut nodes form a disjoint, exhaustive partition of that conditional event, and the conditional expectation of their values is QtY​(x,a)Q_{t}^{Y}(x,a). This includes a terminal child x⊕ax\oplus a, which is itself in the cut. Summing over aa and subtracting VtY​(x)​∑aπt​(a∣x)​ζt​(x,a)=0V_{t}^{Y}(x)\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid x)\zeta_{t}(x,a)=0 gives

∑c∈𝒞hd˙t(c)VtY(c)=∑x∈𝒮:h⁡(x)<hdt(x)𝔥t(x).\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}\dot{d}_{t}(c)V_{t}^{Y}(c)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathcal{S}\,:\,h(x)<h\end{subarray}}d_{t}(x)\mathfrak{h}_{t}(x).

Kernel form and integration. Let atY​(x)=[πt⊙𝒜tY]​(x)a_{t}^{Y}(x)=[\pi_{t}\odot\mathcal{A}_{t}^{Y}](x), extended by zero outside the allowed tokens. Its coordinates sum to zero. Substituting ζt=τ−1​(ea−πt)⊤​vt\zeta_{t}=\tau^{-1}(e_{a}-\pi_{t})^{\top}v_{t} gives

𝔥t​(x)=τ−1​[atY​(x)⊤​vt​(x)−(∑aπt​(a∣x)​𝒜tY​(x,a))​πt⊤​vt​(x)]=τ−1​atY​(x)⊤​vt​(x).\mathfrak{h}_{t}(x)=\tau^{-1}\left[a_{t}^{Y}(x)^{\top}v_{t}(x)-\Bigl(\sum_{a}\pi_{t}(a\mid x)\mathcal{A}_{t}^{Y}(x,a)\Bigr)\pi_{t}^{\top}v_{t}(x)\right]=\tau^{-1}a_{t}^{Y}(x)^{\top}v_{t}(x).

Under raw flow, vt​(x)=∑sKt​(x,s)​Γt​(s)v_{t}(x)=\sum_{s}K_{t}(x,s)\Gamma_{t}(s), proving the bilinear formula. For an actual optimizer path, the same calculation uses vt​(x)=Φt​(x)​θ˙tv_{t}(x)=\Phi_{t}(x)\dot{\theta}_{t}. Integrating the continuous, piecewise differentiable JYJ_{Y} proves the accumulated outcome formula. ∎

The suffix derivative in (**) already includes changes to every downstream prediction. Adding a second derivative of QtYQ_{t}^{Y} to the full decision sum in Equation 21 would just double-count that motion. Conversely, at a fixed cut prefix, V˙tY​(x)\dot{V}_{t}^{Y}(x) cannot generally be replaced by a derivative with respect to the logits at xx alone. Local entropy and terminal correctness are very different observables even though their changes follow the same underlying parameter path.

Reordering the finite source-receiver sum gives the source-resolved form

J˙Y​(t)=∑sμt​(s)​φY,t​(s),φY,t​(s)=1τ​∑xdt​(x)​[πt⊙𝒜tY]​(x)⊤​Kt​(x,s)​Bt​(s).\dot{J}_{Y}(t)=\sum_{s}\mu_{t}(s)\varphi_{Y,t}(s),\qquad\varphi_{Y,t}(s)=\frac{1}{\tau}\sum_{x}d_{t}(x)[\pi_{t}\odot\mathcal{A}_{t}^{Y}](x)^{\top}K_{t}(x,s)B_{t}(s).

A source contributes through every coupled receiver, not just through its own continuation value. The experiments in Appendix E therefore combine prefix dynamics with held-out outcomes.

C.9 Entropy sensitivity and ancestral exposure

Connection to Section 3.3, the entropy-versus-fitting argument. In this subsection Ht(x)=−∑apt(a∣x)logpt(a∣x)H_{t}(x)=-\sum_{a}p_{t}(a\mid x)\log p_{t}(a\mid x) is full-vocabulary model entropy. Its policy is pt=softmax⁡(zt)p_{t}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{t}) at temperature one; the sampling policy in the routing term remains πt\pi_{t} at temperature τ\tau. Fixed-bank evidence is in Section E.3.1.

Proposition C.19 (Entropy sensitivity).

Under Equation 15,

RH​(t)\displaystyle R_{H}(t) =Covνt⁡(Ht​(x),∑j<h⁡(x)ζt​(xj,aj)),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{t}}\!\left(H_{t}(x),\sum_{j<h(x)}\zeta_{t}(x_{j},a_{j})\right), (22)
DH​(t)\displaystyle D_{H}(t) =𝔼νt​[χH,t​(x)⊤​vt​(x)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_{t}}[\chi_{H,t}(x)^{\top}v_{t}(x)],
χH,t​(x)\displaystyle\chi_{H,t}(x) :=∇zHt(x)=−pt(⋅∣x)⊙[logpt(⋅∣x)+Ht(x)𝟏].\displaystyle:=\nabla_{z}H_{t}(x)=-p_{t}(\cdot\mid x)\odot[\log p_{t}(\cdot\mid x)+H_{t}(x)\mathbf{1}].
