H˙t(x)=−Cova∼pt(⋅∣x)(logpt(a∣x),vt(x,a)),|H˙t(x)|≤Varpt⁡(log⁡pt)​Varpt⁡(vt).\dot{H}_{t}(x)=-\operatorname{Cov}_{a\sim p_{t}(\cdot\mid x)}(\log p_{t}(a\mid x),v_{t}(x,a)),\qquad|\dot{H}_{t}(x)|\leq\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{p_{t}}(\log p_{t})\operatorname{Var}_{p_{t}}(v_{t})}. (23)

The parameter-space entropy gradient is Φt​(x)⊤​χH,t​(x)\Phi_{t}(x)^{\top}\chi_{H,t}(x). These identities hold with the actual logit velocity; the raw specialization is vt=Kt​Γtv_{t}=K_{t}\Gamma_{t}.

Proof.

Fix xx and suppress it in the notation. Softmax differentiation gives p˙a=pa​(va−v¯p)\dot{p}_{a}=p_{a}(v_{a}-\bar{v}_{p}), where v¯p=∑apa​va\bar{v}_{p}=\sum_{a}p_{a}v_{a}. Since ∑ap˙a=0\sum_{a}\dot{p}_{a}=0,

H˙\displaystyle\dot{H} =−∑ap˙a(logpa+1)=−∑apa(va−v¯p)logpa\displaystyle=-\sum_{a}\dot{p}_{a}(\log p_{a}+1)=-\sum_{a}p_{a}(v_{a}-\bar{v}_{p})\log p_{a}
=−Covp(logp,v)=−∑apa(logpa+H)va.\displaystyle=-\operatorname{Cov}_{p}(\log p,v)=-\sum_{a}p_{a}(\log p_{a}+H)v_{a}.

The last equality uses ∑apa​log⁡pa=−H\sum_{a}p_{a}\log p_{a}=-H. Since the directional identity holds for every logit direction vv, its coefficient vector is χH=∇zH\chi_{H}=\nabla_{z}H. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz applied to the centered vectors log⁡p−𝔼p​log⁡p\log p-\mathbb{E}_{p}\log p and v−𝔼p​vv-\mathbb{E}_{p}v proves the variance bound. The chain rule gives the parameter gradient Φ⊤​χH\Phi^{\top}\chi_{H}. Finally substitute the local derivative into Proposition C.11; its ancestral score gives the stated RHR_{H} and its fixed-prefix derivative gives DHD_{H}. ∎

Proposition C.20 (Ancestral exposure without first-order entropy increase).

Consider a fixed path of h≥1h\geq 1 binary continue/stop decisions. At every gate, let the conditional continuation probability be a differentiable ct∈(0,1)c_{t}\in(0,1), and hold the suffix executor fixed. Conditional on the path’s starting node, its end is reached with probability cthc_{t}^{h}. With Hbin​(c)=−c​log⁡c−(1−c)​log⁡(1−c)H_{\rm bin}(c)=-c\log c-(1-c)\log(1-c),

∂tlog⁡Prt⁡(reach depth ​h)=h​c˙t/ct,∂tHbin​(ct)=c˙t​log⁡[(1−ct)/ct].\partial_{t}\log\Pr_{t}(\text{reach depth }h)=h\dot{c}_{t}/c_{t},\qquad\partial_{t}H_{\rm bin}(c_{t})=\dot{c}_{t}\log[(1-c_{t})/c_{t}]. (24)
Proof.

The probability of reaching the end is the product of the hh conditional gate probabilities, regardless of any independence interpretation. Its logarithm is h​log⁡cth\log c_{t}, giving the first derivative. Direct differentiation yields Hbin′​(c)=−log⁡c−1+log⁡(1−c)+1=log⁡[(1−c)/c]H_{\rm bin}^{\prime}(c)=-\log c-1+\log(1-c)+1=\log[(1-c)/c]; the chain rule gives the second. ∎

For example, at ct=1/2c_{t}=1/2 with c˙t>0\dot{c}_{t}>0, the reach derivative is positive and each gate’s entropy derivative is zero. Thus a pre-existing uncertain suffix can receive more exposure in the rollout distribution without its predictions becoming flatter.

Checking propensity and teacher-relative discrepancy.

For the fixed WAIT-initiated family 𝒲\mathcal{W}, let wt=pt​(𝒲∣x)∈(0,1)w_{t}=p_{t}(\mathcal{W}\mid x)\in(0,1) at a fixed prefix, bt=log⁡[wt/(1−wt)]b_{t}=\log[w_{t}/(1-w_{t})], and qW=q⁡(𝒲∣x)q_{W}=q(\mathcal{W}\mid x) be fixed. Define

cW(t)=DKL(Ber(qW)∥Ber(wt)).c_{W}(t)=D_{\rm KL}(\operatorname{Ber}(q_{W})\|\operatorname{Ber}(w_{t})).

With the convention 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0 at qW∈{0,1}q_{W}\in\{0,1\},

∂tcW=(wt−qW)​∂tbt.\partial_{t}c_{W}=(w_{t}-q_{W})\partial_{t}b_{t}.

Indeed, writing out the two Bernoulli terms gives ∂wcW=−qW/w+(1−qW)/(1−w)=(w−qW)/[w(1−w)]\partial_{w}c_{W}=-q_{W}/w+(1-q_{W})/(1-w)=(w-q_{W})/[w(1-w)]. Also ∂tbt=w˙t/[wt​(1−wt)]\partial_{t}b_{t}=\dot{w}_{t}/[w_{t}(1-w_{t})]. Multiplication proves the identity, including the endpoint teacher probabilities by the same formula. A decrease in propensity is corrective exactly when its product with the current signed teacher discrepancy is negative; an initially above-teacher class need not remain above the teacher throughout training.

Appendix D Conversion: protocols and additional measurements

This appendix gives the experimental details behind Section 3.2. We first describe the model pairs and the fixed prefixes used for measurement. We then ask where the teachers place their strongest requests, how well those requests produce parameter updates, and how the student’s responsiveness changes during training. The derivations are in Sections C.3 and C.4.

D.1 Setup

We compare two teachers for the same starting student at each scale. At 1.5B, the student is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and the teachers are JustRL-1.5B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. At 7B, the student is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and the teachers are AceReason-Nemotron-7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B. The AIME comparison uses 30 AIME 2024 problems at temperature .6.6. We draw 16 responses per problem at 1.5B and 4 at 7B.

At each scale, eleven rollouts from the initial student provide the prefixes for measurement. Each local kernel is computed from logit gradients with respect to all student parameters. Please note that, computing the gradients is expensive, the eigendecomposition itself is inexpensive. The kernel measurements therefore use sampled positions, while Ξ\Xi serves as a less expensive monitor.

D.2 Where the strongest requests occur

We analyze which kinds of positions receive the strongest teacher requests. The annotated rollouts contain 36,416 positions at 1.5B and 38,168 at 7B. For each teacher, the strongest 1%1\% contains 364 and 381 positions, respectively.

Annotations and enrichment.

We use Opus 5 to label the sentences in the rollouts. Each sentence receives a semantic category, which describes its role in the reasoning. We also classify positions by their location within a sentence and by token kind. These are three separate classifications of the same positions, examined from different semantic aspects. We use the following prompt to create the semantic labels (this rubric is the result of iterating on the model’s reasoning traces a few times, to settle on the most prevalent reasoning categories the model writes in its chain of thought).

For a category cc, enrichment compares its frequency among the teacher’s strongest requests with its frequency among all annotated positions:

Eq​(c)=Pr⁡(c∣strongest ​1%​ under teacher ​q)Pr⁡(c).E_{q}(c)=\frac{\Pr(c\mid\text{strongest }1\%\text{ under teacher }q)}{\Pr(c)}.

A value above 1 means that the category is more common among the strongest requests. For planning, we split the sentences in this class by position: their first three tokens (the opening of a plan) belong to the control family, and the remaining tokens (the stated approach) belong to the technical family; mixed sentences belong to neither. Panel (a) of Figure 3 takes each teacher’s top 50%, 20%, 10%, 5%, 2% and 1% of requests and shows the share of sentence openings (first three tokens), control positions and technical positions, minus the corresponding share among all annotated positions. Figure 9 shows the raw shares. Bootstrap intervals resample the annotated rollouts. They are computed separately for each teacher. Panels (b, c) of Figure 3 show twelve selected rows, and Figure 10 shows the full set. Table 1 gives the values used in the main figure.

Differences between teachers.

At 1.5B, planning openings are enriched 3.59×3.59\times under the sibling teacher and 0.30×0.30\times under the larger teacher. Sentence-initial positions are enriched 2.91×2.91\times and 1.46×1.46\times, respectively. At 7B, the sibling teacher places relatively more of its strongest requests at reframing, checking, and doubt positions. Wait-family tokens are enriched 4.50×4.50\times under the sibling and 1.23×1.23\times under the larger teacher.

The difference depends on the category. At 7B, planning openings are enriched 4.13×4.13\times and 1.06×1.06\times, while the stated approach of a plan is enriched 0.72×0.72\times and 1.70×1.70\times; the teachers’ derivation enrichment is similar (0.84×0.84\times and 0.83×0.83\times). Digit-bearing positions are relatively more prominent under the larger teacher at both scales.

We find that, as the percentile goes up, the sibling teacher’s shares of sentence openings and control positions grow relative to all positions, while the larger teacher’s return to or fall below them (Figure 9). Among the strongest 1%, the sibling teacher’s share of sentence openings exceeds the larger teacher’s by 19.219.2 [13.113.1, 27.727.7] percentage points at 1.5B and 27.627.6 [18.818.8, 37.037.0] at 7B.

D.3 Conversion estimates by semantic class

We now ask which factors in Equation 4 distinguish the healthy and stalled runs. We report pressure PP, accessibility AA, and coherence CC separately for the control and technical samples selected for each teacher. The initial comparison asks how the same starting student responds to the two teachers. The endpoint comparison asks how much disagreement remains and how the student’s responsiveness has changed.

Measurement and estimation.

We save the training rollouts and the request vector BB computed at every position during training. The initial requests B0B_{0} used in the frozen-request probes come directly from these records. For a fixed request at prefix ss, the parameter gradient is gt​(s)=Φt​(s)⊤​B​(s)g_{t}(s)=\Phi_{t}(s)^{\top}B(s). We obtain it by backpropagating through B​(s)⊤​zt​(s)B(s)^{\top}z_{t}(s) while holding B⁡(s)B(s) constant.

The squared norm of a sample mean includes sampling variance. We correct for this before estimating coherence. For n>1n>1 sampled gradients, write g¯=n−1​∑igi\bar{g}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}g_{i} and D^g=n−1​∑i‖gi‖2\widehat{D}_{g}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\|g_{i}\|^{2}. The correction is

C^corr=(‖g¯‖2−[D^g−‖g¯‖2]/(n−1))+D^g,D^g>0,\widehat{C}_{\mathrm{corr}}=\frac{\left(\|\bar{g}\|^{2}-[\widehat{D}_{g}-\|\bar{g}\|^{2}]/(n-1)\right)_{+}}{\widehat{D}_{g}},\qquad\widehat{D}_{g}>0,

where (r)+=max⁡(r,0)(r)_{+}=\max(r,0). Under independent sampling, the numerator before truncation is unbiased for the squared norm of the population-mean gradient (Proposition C.9).

Initial comparison.

Table 2 shows why gradient norm alone does not explain conversion. At 7B, the healthy run has somewhat lower accessibility but 2.752.75–3.24×3.24\times higher coherence across the two classes. Its collective gain is 2.272.27–2.62×2.62\times higher. The stalled run still has a comparable or larger gradient norm because its request pressure is higher.

At 1.5B, accessibility is similar between the two teachers, and the coherence difference depends on the class. The initial collective gains are nearly equal in control: 1.621.62 versus 1.651.65, in units of 10310^{3}. In technical, the healthy run has the larger gain: 3.493.49 versus 2.102.10. Thus its larger gradient norms do not imply a larger conversion gain in every class.

Remaining requests and responsiveness.

Table 3 separates two endpoint comparisons. The live conversion factors use the current requests BtB_{t}. They measure the response to the remaining disagreements with the teacher. The last column instead reapplies the initial requests B0B_{0}. With both the requests and prefixes fixed, this column measures how local responsiveness to those requests has changed.

The healthy runs retain only 0.50.5–1.5%1.5\% of their initial request energy. The stalled runs retain 60.260.2–79.0%79.0\%. Meanwhile, accessibility to the initial requests increases in both classes of each healthy run and decreases in both classes of each stalled run.

D.4 How the local kernel changes

To understand the change in responsiveness, we measure both the strength and movement of the kernel’s leading directions. At each prefix ss, let Vt,3​(s)V_{t,3}(s) contain the orthonormal eigenvectors of the symmetrized local kernel Kt​(s,s)K_{t}(s,s) with the three largest eigenvalues. Denote those eigenvalues by {λj,t​(s)}j=13\{\lambda_{j,t}(s)\}_{j=1}^{3}. Main Figure 4(b) plots

G3​(s,t)=∑j=13λj,t​(s)∑j=13λj,0​(s),O3​(s,t)=‖V0,3​(s)⊤​Vt,3​(s)‖F23.G_{3}(s,t)=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{3}\lambda_{j,t}(s)}{\sum_{j=1}^{3}\lambda_{j,0}(s)},\qquad O_{3}(s,t)=\frac{\|V_{0,3}(s)^{\top}V_{t,3}(s)\|_{F}^{2}}{3}.

G3G_{3} measures the change in the sum of the three largest eigenvalues. O3O_{3} measures how much their subspace overlaps with its initial position. It is the mean squared cosine of the three principal angles: 11 means identical subspaces and 00 means orthogonal subspaces. The main figure reports median G3G_{3} and O3O_{3} over 160 positions; the table below reports 1−O31-O_{3} instead. Moreover, subspace movement alone does not tell us whether the kernel becomes better or worse aligned with the teacher’s requests. For this, we measure the share of the initial request in the leading subspace, w1:3(s,t)=∑j≤3|vj,t⊤b0|2w_{1:3}(s,t)=\sum_{j\leq 3}|v_{j,t}^{\top}b_{0}|^{2}, where b0b_{0} is the unit direction of the initial request. Its change is Δw1:3\Delta w_{1:3}. Figure 4(c) compares this change for the two teachers’ requests in the same checkpoint kernel.

Early on in training (by step 50), the healthy 1.5B run has already changed its leading subspace, while the leading strength is near its initial value. The strength increases later. The healthy 7B run mainly increases leading strength, with little subspace movement. Both stalled runs lose leading strength.

The table also distinguishes a typical position from an average weighted by request energy. For example, at step 50 of healthy 1.5B, the median sensitivity ratio is 1.191.19, while the ratio of weighted accessibilities is 3.953.95. The latter gives more weight to positions with larger initial requests. Their difference reflects the weighting and the way results are combined across positions.

Figure 12 extends the comparison to the full eigenvalue profile. It compares eigenvalues at the same sorted rank across checkpoints. It is clear that the healthy runs experience a lift in the principal eigenvalues as training proceeds, while the stalled runs experience a decline instead.

A separate comparison groups initial directions by their request energy. The reported growth is not concentrated in the groups with stronger requests. We therefore distinguish a turn toward the teacher’s requests from preferential growth along the most strongly requested initial directions.

D.5 Alignment with the teacher

The leading subspace rotates in the healthy 1.5B run. Does this movement favor the teacher that trained the student? We compare the training-run teacher’s initial requests with the other teacher’s initial requests at the same prefixes and token coordinates. Both are evaluated in the same checkpoint kernel. More precisely, at each position, we subtract their changes in projection onto the leading subspace:

ds(t)=Δw1:3trained(s,t)−Δw1:3other(s,t).d_{s}(t)=\Delta w_{1:3}^{\mathrm{trained}}(s,t)-\Delta w_{1:3}^{\mathrm{other}}(s,t).

A positive value means that the training teacher’s requests gain more projection. Figure 4(c) uses step 50 for all four runs. The comparison holds the kernel change fixed and asks which field gains more projection.

The healthy 1.5B run has a median paired difference of 1.791.79 percentage points, with a 95%95\% interval of [0.94,3.13][0.94,3.13]. The other three intervals include zero. These measurements show that there is a “preferential” turn toward the training teacher’s requests in healthy 1.5B. The paired median need not equal the difference between the two separate medians: 5.49−2.425.49-2.42 and 1.791.79 summarize the same positions in different orders. The bootstrap measures variation across the sampled rollouts with the trained checkpoints fixed.

Appendix E Broadcast: protocols and additional measurements

This appendix gives the experimental details for Section 3.3. We examine how OPD changes prefix visitation and the student’s predictions on fixed prefixes. We then ask whether the student can complete its reasoning from those prefixes and reach a correct answer. The theoretical backbone is derived and presented in Sections C.5, C.6, C.7, C.8 and C.9.

E.1 Models and measurement setup

Models and training.

All three learners use JustRL-1.5B as the teacher. The strong learner is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B which we also studied in Section 3.2. The unprepared learner is Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. “Prepared Qwen” starts from the same Qwen 1.5B instruct model after four passes of offline distillation on OpenMathInstruct2 (see the preparation section, Appendix F for more details). The Qwen runs use 200 training steps, 256 rollouts per update, temperature 1.0, and an 8,192-token generation cap. DeepSeek’s generation cap is 4,096 tokens.

Rollout banks.

We save 32 rollouts from each batch ℓ∈{1,21,41,…,161,181,196}\ell\in\{1,21,41,\ldots,161,181,196\}. A bank is this fixed set of rollout texts. Batch ℓ\ell is generated after ℓ−1\ell-1 updates. Thus batch 41 appears at update 40 in the routing and drift plots. Checkpoint 0 is each learner’s starting model, including the offline-prepared model for prepared Qwen.

When does the model initiate checking?

The WAIT family 𝒲\mathcal{W} contains the 13 tokens that decode to “wait” (after whitespace is removed and text is lowercased). We examine candidate sentence starts: the first response position and positions after a token ending in a period, question mark, exclamation mark, colon, or newline. The student and teacher probabilities of this family are denoted as wt​(x)=pt​(𝒲∣x)w_{t}(x)=p_{t}(\mathcal{W}\mid x) and qW​(x)=q​(𝒲∣x)q_{W}(x)=q(\mathcal{W}\mid x). We measure the mean log⁡wt\log w_{t} across candidate starts. For the above- and below-teacher comparisons, we use log-odds bt=log⁡[wt/(1−wt)]b_{t}=\log[w_{t}/(1-w_{t})] and bq=log⁡[qW/(1−qW)]b_{q}=\log[q_{W}/(1-q_{W})].

We form the two groups using a reference checkpoint rr: checkpoint 0 for DeepSeek and checkpoint 20 for the Qwen learners. We include a prefix only if max⁡(wr,qW)≥10−3\max(w_{r},q_{W})\geq 10^{-3} and |br−bq|≥0.5|b_{r}-b_{q}|\geq 0.5. The sign of br−bqb_{r}-b_{q} determines whether the student initially assigns more or less probability than the teacher. Each prefix keeps the same group at every evaluated checkpoint.

We also count emitted WAIT tokens per thousand response tokens, and measure the arithmetic mean of wtw_{t} at candidate starts. These quantities answer different questions. The emission rate counts what the model actually generates. Mean probability and mean log probability describe its actual predictions at the selected prefixes.

To assess agreement with the teacher, we use the binary discrepancy cW=DKL(Ber(qW)∥Ber(wt))c_{W}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\operatorname{Ber}(q_{W})\,\|\,\operatorname{Ber}(w_{t})\right). At a fixed prefix, ∂tcW=(wt−qW)​∂tbt\partial_{t}c_{W}=(w_{t}-q_{W})\partial_{t}b_{t}. Lowering WAIT probability improves agreement only while the student’s probability is above the teacher’s.

E.2 DeepSeek: adjusting the probability of checking

DeepSeek’s local loss falls mainly because its predictions change at fixed prefixes (Table 6). We next ask whether these changes bring its checking probabilities closer to the teacher’s, as“wait”-initiated checking / backtracking is a dominant part of the model’s reasoning traces and observed to initiate sentences in which the model manage its epistemic states (Marjanovic et al., 2026). We use the classes in Section E.1, defined by whether the reference student’s WAIT probability lies above or below the teacher’s.

In the first 512 tokens, the above-teacher class has ∑R^=0.036\sum\widehat{R}=0.036 and ∑D^=−1.824\sum\widehat{D}=-1.824. The below-teacher class has 0.5050.505 and 1.9181.918, respectively. The drift contribution therefore lowers mean checking log-odds in the first class and raises them in the second. The main plot uses filled circles and open triangles for these two classes. Routing can still be large within individual intervals, even when its contributions partly cancel over training.

We check whether this two-sided adjustment reduces the discrepancy from the teacher on a fixed set of prefixes (Table 7). For DeepSeek, the discrepancy falls from 0.07890.0789 to 0.00320.0032 in the above-teacher class and from 0.19150.1915 to 0.01490.0149 in the below-teacher class. Interestingly, the same comparison on held-out prepared-Qwen text gives decreases from about 0.0390.039 to 0.0140.014 and from 0.2930.293 to 0.0390.039, so the improvement even extends beyond DeepSeek’s own generated prefixes.

To examine how closely the changes follow the teacher, we regress the change in student log-odds on the teacher and reference-student log-odds. On DeepSeek’s own prefixes at checkpoint 200, the teacher coefficient is about 0.900.90, the reference-student coefficient about −0.88-0.88, and R2R^{2} about 0.940.94. This detailed relation is much weaker on the held-out Qwen prefixes. The fixed-prefix results support improved calibration on both sets, but the closer match to the teacher’s pattern occurs on DeepSeek’s own text.

E.3 Unprepared Qwen 1.5B: fitting on changing prefixes

For unprepared Qwen, the local loss decreases (0.579→0.0730.579\to 0.073). The accumulated contributions are ∑R^L=+0.474\sum\widehat{R}_{L}=+0.474 and ∑D^L=−0.980\sum\widehat{D}_{L}=-0.980. Thus changes in predictions at fixed prefixes account for the decrease, while changes in prefix visitation raise the loss. This balance varies during training. In the first comparison at step 20, loss rises by +0.268+0.268: routing contributes +0.455+0.455, which exceeds the decrease from drift, −0.187-0.187. Later on, loss mainly falls through changes dominated by drift, as the main text already pointed out. The large rise in entropy has a different origin: it comes mainly from prefix visitation, as shown in the main text.

E.3.1 Loss and entropy on the same prefixes

The preceding comparisons use batches generated at different training steps. We now hold the prefixes fixed to see what the student learns on the same text. We use the prefixes from batch 41. (The entropy-response identity, how it can change through routing without significant drift, and examples are discussed in the theory presented in Section C.9.)

On these prefixes, student entropy falls from 4.9874.987 nats at initialization to 3.9893.989 at checkpoint 160. The local loss falls from 0.7890.789 to 0.0570.057. Teacher entropy is 2.8592.859 nats, below both student values. The teacher is more uncertain here than on the coherent initial text, but the student still learns sharper predictions on these prefixes.

These measurements answer different questions. The falling loss shows fitting at fixed prefixes. The entropy decomposition shows that the large rise in uncertainty mainly reflects which prefixes the model visits. Note that these are primarily examinations of how the local per-prefix readouts change. To understand how the learnt model’s continuations reach a correct answer we need to probe their continuation advantages which involve non-local readouts, as Equation 21 shows. We examine this next.

E.4 Continuation value at the unprepared student’s answer boundaries

We now examine prefixes at which the initial student was about to answer. Holding these prefixes fixed lets us ask two questions: how does training change the probability of answering now, and how successful are the continuations from the two alternatives? This comparison isolates changes at the selected prefixes from changes in prefix visitation.

Prefix selection and continuation conditions.

We sample two rollouts per problem from the initial student on 50 held-out MATH-500 problems. “Cutting” the rollout immediately before a final-answer marker (\boxed or Answer:) gives 86 prefixes. We evaluate the initial student, checkpoints 20–200 of the unprepared run, and the JustRL teacher on these same prefixes. For each model, we record the next-token probability mass π\pi on the probe’s answer class.

We draw six continuations per prefix under each of three conditions: the answer condition forces the answer token, the “continue” condition forces the model’s most probable non-answer token, and the “natural” condition samples without forcing either token. All conditions use temperature 0.60.6, top-p=0.95p=0.95, and a cap of 16,38416{,}384 new tokens. Table 8 reports the fraction of correct continuations.

Branch probabilities and continuation values.

Let QansQ_{\rm ans} and QcontQ_{\rm cont} denote the correctness values of the two forced branches, “answer” vs “continue” (recall that QQ denotes the continuation success rate from the given prefix distribution after forcing an action choice). Their probability-weighted probe value is V=π​Qans+(1−π)​QcontV=\pi Q_{\rm ans}+(1-\pi)Q_{\rm cont}. This value’s change relative to the initial student decomposes as

Δ​V=Δ​π​(Q¯ans−Q¯cont)⏟changed branch probability+π¯​Δ​Qans+(1−π¯)​Δ​Qcont⏟changed branch values,\Delta V=\underbrace{\Delta\pi\,(\bar{Q}_{\rm ans}-\bar{Q}_{\rm cont})}_{\text{changed branch probability}}+\underbrace{\bar{\pi}\,\Delta Q_{\rm ans}+(1-\bar{\pi})\,\Delta Q_{\rm cont}}_{\text{changed branch values}},

where bars denote the average of the two endpoint values at the same prefix. The first term describes moving probability between the two branches. It is positive when probability moves toward the more successful branch. The second term describes changes in the branch continuation values. We calculate both terms at each prefix before averaging, and obtain intervals from 2,0002{,}000 bootstrap draws over prefixes. Note that this split applies to the two forced branches. The most probable non-answer token can differ between models. The continue-branch value therefore includes both that first choice and the later continuation. Natural continuations are sampled separately, and their success rate need not equal VV.

How the results change during training.

Early on, at update 20, the mean log-odds of answering have fallen from +2.4+2.4 to −3.9-3.9. Yet the answer and continue branches have similar correctness, 0.300.30 and 0.290.29. The early shift toward continuing is therefore not yet accompanied by lower continuation success on these prefixes.

By update 100, the answer branch still succeeds with probability 0.340.34, but the continue branch succeeds with probability 0.030.03. Natural continuations succeed with probability 0.060.06. The 8%8\% answer-producing rate in the main text is for the continue branch. It counts any answer, whereas 3%3\% counts a correct answer. Both terms in the two-branch decomposition are negative at this checkpoint. On balance, probability moves toward the less successful branch. Changes in branch values also reduce the probe value. Success partly recovers by update 200, but natural-continuation correctness remains below its initial value.

The teacher also favors continuing over answering on these prefixes. Its continue branch, however, is more successful than its answer branch (0.580.58 versus 0.420.42), and its natural continuations succeed with probability 0.600.60. This illustrates the role of continuation values in Equation 9. In the probability term, a shift toward continuing helps when continuing is more successful than answering now. These answer-boundary probes examine that relation on fixed prefixes. Section E.7 then uses fixed reference continuers to examine changes in prefix visitation.

E.5 Prepared Qwen: how checking changes during training

The prepared run improves its held-out score, even though its rollouts change markedly early in training. We first examine the order of these changes. We then ask whether the later decrease in checking also occurs on unchanged prefixes, how the teacher’s requests change, and which representative “calibration errors” remain.

The order of the early changes.

Entropy rises early on. At step 20, entropy increases from 2.172.17 to 4.334.33 nats. Routing contributes +1.98+1.98 and drift +0.18+0.18, while local loss falls from 0.7070.707 to 0.1730.173. In the next comparison, from batch 21 to batch 41, loss overshoots to 0.4370.437. Its routing contribution is +0.363+0.363 and its drift contribution −0.099-0.099. Entropy on batch 41 is already low (about 0.700.70 nats), and remains low (about 0.60.6–0.90.9) on later batches. Thus the loss overshoot follows the initial entropy rise. It mainly reflects a change in prefix visitation, similar to the early phase of the unprepared run.

The WAIT emission rate also rises and then falls (Figure 14, middle). To see whether the model changes its predictions on the same prefixes, we evaluate each checkpoint on the candidate sentence starts in the first 512 tokens of batch 41 (Figure 15, left). Mean WAIT probability rises from 0.04940.0494 at checkpoint 20 to 0.11300.1130 at checkpoint 50. It then falls to 0.08420.0842 at checkpoint 100 and is 0.08740.0874 at checkpoint 160. The later decrease therefore includes a change in predictions on unchanged prefixes. The probability remains above its level at checkpoint 20.

Mean log-WAIT probability gives another view of the change across rollout batches (Figure 14, right). Drift is positive in the first comparison (+0.56+0.56) and negative by checkpoint 50 (−1.25-1.25). Routing is positive during the expansion (+2.89+2.89). Further decreases from drift accumulate through checkpoint 100. Later changes, including much of the decline between batches 121 and 141, mainly come from prefix visitation. These contributions sum to a change in mean log probability, not in emitted frequency. On some other fixed prefix sets, mean log probability and arithmetic mean probability change in opposite directions. We therefore keep these measurements separate.

How the teacher’s requests change.

Overall, the requests change from favoring WAIT to suppressing it on average. More specifically, we examine requests at sampled WAIT occurrences in full training batches (Figure 15, right). The mean request is about +0.19+0.19 to +0.26+0.26 at batches 10–25, with intervals above zero. At batch 50, it is −0.0418-0.0418 (95% interval [−0.0635,−0.0182][-0.0635,-0.0182]), and 0.5280.528 of the sampled requests are negative. Later means are nearer zero.

Remaining calibration errors.

We finally ask whether these changes bring checking probabilities closer to the teacher’s. The prefix classes are fixed at checkpoint 20, and we compare checkpoints 20 and 200 on the same pooled prefix set (Table 7). The discrepancy increases from 0.02760.0276 to 0.05800.0580 in the above-teacher class. It decreases from 0.56270.5627 to 0.38130.3813 in the below-teacher class. On average, calibration improves only in the initially below-teacher class.

Over-use also grows within the above-teacher subset with qW≥0.05q_{W}\geq 0.05. Mean student probability rises approximately 0.33→0.500.33\to 0.50 on its own text and 0.29→0.460.29\to 0.46 on held-out text, against teacher probability about 0.150.15. The changes still depend on teacher probability after accounting for the reference student’s probability, including on held-out prefixes. Thus the student’s adjustments remain related to the teacher, but the calibration improvement appears imperfect and weaker than the DeepSeek run.

E.6 Uncertainty across rollout depths

We next examine when uncertainty rises and where it appears in the response. Figure 16 uses full training batches from the unprepared Qwen run. Each training update samples 256 rollouts on DAPO prompts at temperature one, with an 8,192-token generation cap.

The left heatmap reports student surprisal: the negative log probability of the token the student generated. The right heatmap reports the teacher’s highest next-token probability at the same prefix. Surprisal uses the sampled token, whereas the entropy measurements above use the full next-token distribution. The heatmaps summarize 512-token windows. Rows index rollout batches, including those labeled “tape step” in the main figure. Batch ℓ\ell follows ℓ−1\ell-1 updates. Hatched cells and table dashes indicate that no value is reported there, as the model does not reach that generation length yet.

Table 9 gives two example windows. Between batches 20 and 35, surprisal at positions 1536–2047 rises from 3.243.24 to 6.476.47 nats. In the first 512 tokens, it rises only from 0.620.62 to 0.900.90. Teacher top-1 probability falls from 0.510.51 to 0.290.29 in the deeper window, compared with 0.810.81 to 0.780.78 in the front window. Thus the early increase in uncertainty is much larger in the deeper of these two windows. The change is not monotone: deep-window surprisal falls to 3.193.19 by batch 100. Our main routing and drift analysis ends at batch 161.

E.7 Fixed-reference continuation experiments

The answer-versus-continue experiment in Section E.4 conducted a case study probing continuation from fixed prefixes. This, however, is not enough in understanding the decline in terminal score of the trained student model. Recall that, at a high level, the broadcast not only affects continuation behaviors of the model, but also changes its prefix visitation probabilities. Therefore, to understand the terminal-score decline during OPD, we must also consider how the prefixes that the student checkpoints generates as training proceeds. At any rollout depth, successful completion depends on two quantities: which prefixes the student reaches, and how successfully it continues from those prefixes. We first express terminal score in terms of these two quantities, then show how the reference-policy experiment separates their changes.

Prefix visitation and continuation.

Fix a cut depth hh. Recall our notation from before, that dt​(x)d_{t}(x) is the probability that checkpoint tt reaches prefix xx, and VtY​(x)V_{t}^{Y}(x) is its expected terminal score when it completes that prefix. The set of rollout cuts 𝒞h\mathcal{C}_{h} includes depth-hh prefixes and responses that ended earlier (an earlier completed response just retains its terminal score). Conditioning on 𝒞h\mathcal{C}_{h} gives

JY​(t)=∑x∈𝒞hdt​(x)​VtY​(x).J_{Y}(t)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}d_{t}(x)V_{t}^{Y}(x).

This is just the usual average over the “continuation problems” presented to the student by its own generation. Training changes both the weights dtd_{t} and the continuation values VtYV_{t}^{Y}. Comparing each checkpoint’s prefixes using that checkpoint as the continuer therefore only measures their combined effect.

Hold the continuer fixed.

Using the initial student as the reference, add and subtract ∑x∈𝒞hdt​(x)​V0Y​(x)\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}d_{t}(x)V_{0}^{Y}(x) to obtain

JY​(t)−JY​(0)\displaystyle J_{Y}(t)-J_{Y}(0) =∑x∈𝒞h[dt​(x)−d0​(x)]​V0Y​(x)⏟prefix visitation, evaluated by the initial continuer+∑x∈𝒞hdt​(x)​[VtY​(x)−V0Y​(x)]⏟continuation change on the same current prefixes.\displaystyle=\underbrace{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}[d_{t}(x)-d_{0}(x)]V_{0}^{Y}(x)}_{\text{prefix visitation, evaluated by the initial continuer}}\quad+\underbrace{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}d_{t}(x)[V_{t}^{Y}(x)-V_{0}^{Y}(x)]}_{\text{continuation change on the same current prefixes}}. (25)

The first term compares the initial and trained prefix distributions while keeping the continuer fixed. A negative value means that the initial student finds the trained prefixes harder to finish than its own prefixes. The second term keeps the trained prefix distribution fixed and compares the two continuers. A negative value means that the trained student is less successful than the initial student on those same prefixes. Thus the comparison changes the prefix-generating policy first, then the continuing policy.

Our experiment implements the intermediate case directly: checkpoint tt generates the first hh tokens, and the initial student completes the rest of the rollout. Let us write its expected score as

Ft0​(h)=∑x∈𝒞hdt​(x)​V0Y​(x).F_{t}^{0}(h)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}d_{t}(x)V_{0}^{Y}(x). (26)

The two terms in Equation 25 are therefore Ft0​(h)−JY​(0)F_{t}^{0}(h)-J_{Y}(0) and JY​(t)−Ft0​(h)J_{Y}(t)-F_{t}^{0}(h). They can be estimated by averaging completed responses. The first supplies a common measure of prefix difficulty across checkpoints; the second compares continuers on each checkpoint’s own prefix distribution.

Experimental setup and results.

The study uses 250 held-out MATH problems, two source rollouts per problem from each of checkpoints 50, 100, and 200, and cuts at 256, 512, and 1,024 response tokens. Each active prefix is continued four times by the generating checkpoint, the initial student, and the teacher. All continuers receive the remainder of an 8,192-token total response budget. The readout is extracted-answer success on the full prefix and continuation; the answer need not be immediately followed by an end-of-turn token. Stopping is recorded separately. The estimator averages continuation scores within each prefix, then over the two source rollouts and uniformly over problems, retaining earlier completed responses as above. This population and budget differ from those of the selected answer-boundary probe in Section E.4. The reported values below are rounded sample means; independently sampled self-continuations estimate the same JY​(t)J_{Y}(t) but need not give identical means at different cuts.

Consider the 256-token cut at step 50. The initial student scores 48.4%48.4\% on its own rollouts and 50.5%50.5\% when it completes the trained checkpoint’s prefixes. The trained checkpoint scores 39.5%39.5\% on those same prefixes. The first comparison therefore contributes +2.1+2.1 percentage points, while the second contributes −11.0-11.0 points, accounting for the total −8.9-8.9-point difference. At this cut, the prefixes remain usable by the initial student; the trained student loses performance in completing them.

Table 10 shows that at step 50, the initial continuer already scores lower on deep prefixes: the 1,024-token contrast is −8.1-8.1 points. At later checkpoints, the deficit also reaches the shallow cuts, while the 1,024-token deficit remains similar in magnitude. On the 256-token prefixes, the trained-minus-initial continuation contrast remains negative at steps 100 and 200 (−12.1-12.1 and −6.2-6.2 points). By step 200, both terms in Equation 25 are negative: the initial student finds the new prefixes harder, and the trained student completes those prefixes less successfully than the initial student.

Connection to Equation 9.

The same two factors describe the instantaneous dynamics. Differentiating the cut identity gives

J˙Y​(t)=∑x∈𝒞hd˙t​(x)​VtY​(x)+∑x∈𝒞hdt​(x)​V˙tY​(x).\dot{J}_{Y}(t)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}\dot{d}_{t}(x)V_{t}^{Y}(x)+\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{h}}d_{t}(x)\dot{V}_{t}^{Y}(x). (27)

Under the regularity assumptions in Proposition C.18, the first term computes the contributions to Equation 9 from decisions before the cut, and the second collects those from the cut onward. Both arise from the same shared parameter update. If the reference is checkpoint tt instead of checkpoint 0, and the compared policy is an infinitesimally later checkpoint t+d​tt+dt, the differences in Equation 25 (divided by elapsed training time) recover the derivative, hence recovering these two terms. Such measurements are unrealistic to implement and too noisy to measure in practice, however, so our experiment instead use the initial policy as the reference continuer to magnify the trend of visited-prefix quality / continuation difficulty.

What does moving the cut measure?

Another interesting question is, at a fixed checkpoint tt, moving the rollout cut from h1h_{1} to h2h_{2} lets the trained student generate an additional block of tokens before the initial student takes over. A decrease in Ft0F_{t}^{0} means that this additional trained-student generation leaves the initial continuer less able to reach a correct answer. To connect it to continuation advantages, let us follow the initial student’s value along a trained rollout. For each action decision, 𝒜0Y​(xj,aj)=V0Y​(xj+1)−V0Y​(xj)\mathcal{A}_{0}^{Y}(x_{j},a_{j})=V_{0}^{Y}(x_{j+1})-V_{0}^{Y}(x_{j}). Summing over a block yields a telescoping series over depth of the cuts, then averaging over the rollouts gives

Ft0(h2)−Ft0(h1)=∑x∈𝒮h1≤h⁡(x)<h2dt(x)𝔼a∼πt(⋅∣x)[𝒜0Y(x,a)].F_{t}^{0}(h_{2})-F_{t}^{0}(h_{1})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathcal{S}\\ h_{1}\leq h(x)<h_{2}\end{subarray}}d_{t}(x)\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid x)}[\mathcal{A}_{0}^{Y}(x,a)]. (28)

Here 𝒮\mathcal{S} contains decision prefixes; completed responses contribute no further decisions and retain their scores. At depth zero, the initial student generates the whole response, so Ft0​(0)=JY​(0)F_{t}^{0}(0)=J_{Y}(0). At the total response cap, the trained student has generated the whole response, so Ft0​(Hmax)=JY​(t)F_{t}^{0}(H_{\max})=J_{Y}(t). Consequently, the differences across any partition of the full response sum to JY​(t)−JY​(0)J_{Y}(t)-J_{Y}(0). Fixed cuts therefore measure aggregate contributions of token blocks to this finite policy comparison, using completed outcomes in place of separate continuation-value estimates at every token.

Appendix F Preparation: protocols and additional measurements

F.1 Three-family AIME comparison

Students and teachers.

The pairs are Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct / JustRL-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct / AceReason-Nemotron-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct / Llama-3.1-Nemotron-Nano-8B-v1. Each pair shares a tokenizer vocabulary. The fixed teacher supplies the preparation text, the offline-control targets, and the on-policy log-probabilities. The Llama teacher uses its reasoning mode with the system prompt “detailed thinking on.”

Stage 1: offline preparation on OMI2.

Each teacher generates solutions to problems drawn from OpenMathInstruct-2 (Toshniwal et al., 2024), at temperature one with an 8,192-token response cap. The student uses token-level forward KL on the teacher’s recorded top-16 next-token support. The plotted cold start uses 512 optimizer steps of 256 sequences, or 131,072 sequence presentations. The Qwen 1.5B, 7B and Llama corpora each contain 32,768 teacher solutions, so this is four corpus sweeps.

The offline settings are AdamW, learning rate 10−610^{-6}, momentum coefficients (0.9,0.95)(0.9,0.95), no weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.0. The cold-start sequence limit is 8,192 tokens.

Stage 2: DAPO comparisons.

The prompt pool is DAPO-Math-17k (Yu et al., 2025), recorded as 17,398 unique problems. Training uses consecutive blocks of 6,400 rows in the released ordering. Each block contains 6,235–6,318 unique problems.

OPD samples four student responses for each of 64 prompts per step, giving 256 responses and one optimizer step per update. Sampling is at temperature one, capped at 8,192 tokens for Qwen and 14,336 for Llama.

The offline continuation instead uses four teacher-generated solutions for each prompt row in the same blocks: 25,600 sequences per 6,400-row block. It uses the teacher forward-KL objective and optimizer settings as preparation, at 256 sequences per step. The sequence limits are 8,192 for Qwen and 15,360 for Llama, the latter retaining the reported teacher solutions generated with a 14,336-token response cap. Thus the comparison matches the implemented offline and on-policy recipes in prompt blocks, sequence counts, and total optimizer steps.

Evaluation and sampled coverage.

The evaluation pools AIME 2024 and 2025, 30 problems each. Each checkpoint is evaluated using 32 responses per problem from the first sampling batch (batch a), with vLLM, the student’s template, temperature 0.60.6, top-p=0.95p=0.95, and a 16,384-new-token cap. Scoring is lenient: answer extraction uses a boxed answer when present, otherwise an explicit answer marker including “the answer is”.

Following Chen et al. (2021), if cic_{i} of the 32 responses solve problem ii, we estimate

pass​@​k^=160​∑i=160[1−(32−cik)(32k)],1≤k≤32,\widehat{\mathrm{pass@}k}=\frac{1}{60}\sum_{i=1}^{60}\left[1-\frac{\binom{32-c_{i}}{k}}{\binom{32}{k}}\right],\qquad 1\leq k\leq 32, (29)

with a zero numerator when 32−ci<k32-c_{i}<k. In particular, pass@1 is the average observed success rate, and pass@32 is the fraction solved at least once in the sample. A problem never solved in 32 attempts can still lie within the model’s support, and one solved on all 32 attempts can still have success probability below one.

The lower panels plot the empirical survival curve 60−1∑i𝟏{ci/32≥r}60^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{c_{i}/32\geq r\} for r>0r>0. Its limit as r↓0r\downarrow 0 is observed coverage and its area on [0,1][0,1] is the average solve rate. At exactly r=0r=0, the literal weak-inequality expression equals one; the plotted left endpoint represents the positive-threshold limit. These are marginal distributions across problems.

Endpoints and paired problem changes.

Table 12 gives the pooled pass@kk endpoints and the number of problems at each empirical reliability threshold.

Among problems solved at least once by both the OPD and offline endpoints, mean observed success rates (OPD/offline) are 0.281/0.1040.281/0.104 for Qwen 1.5B (3 problems), 0.599/0.4550.599/0.455 for Qwen 7B (25), and 0.264/0.1590.264/0.159 for Llama (13). These intersections are selected using both arms’ samples, so their means are descriptive. Against the offline endpoint, OPD gains coverage on 8, 11, and 8 problems and loses it on 2, 1, and 1, respectively.

Uncertainty.

For each student and year, we resample the 30 problem indices with replacement, keeping the OPD and offline outcomes paired. For pass@1 the per-problem difference is (ciOPD−cioffline)/32(c_{i}^{\mathrm{OPD}}-c_{i}^{\mathrm{offline}})/32; for pass@32 it is 𝟏{ciOPD>0}−𝟏{cioffline>0}\mathbf{1}\{c_{i}^{\mathrm{OPD}}>0\}-\mathbf{1}\{c_{i}^{\mathrm{offline}}>0\}. Table 13 reports the mean difference and the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of its exact conditional bootstrap distribution, computed by convolution of the empirical per-problem difference distribution. This avoids Monte Carlo error in the interval endpoints. The intervals quantify problem-resampling uncertainty conditional on the checkpoints and recorded outcomes.

F.2 Preparation-dose study

We follow the same preparation (cold start) procedure as before, except we vary the number of passes over the cold-start corpus and study subsequent OPD performance. Evaluation uses the first 250 MATH-500 problems, four responses per problem, temperature 0.60.6, top-p=0.95p=0.95, a 16,384-new-token cap, and the deployment template. Table 14 reports strict pass@1 and 95% problem-bootstrap intervals with 2,000 resamples.

The 1.5B OPD series uses the step-100 checkpoint. The 7B series uses the best checkpoint evaluated every ten steps within the first 100 OPD steps: steps 30, 50, and 90 for one, two, and four preparation passes, respectively. Its intervals are computed at the selected checkpoint and do not adjust for checkpoint selection.
